lore.name: Air Nomads
lore.info: The Air Nomads lived in four temples high in the mountains, one at each point of the compass, and every one of them was an airbender. Children were raised by the monks rather than by their parents, and the people were led by the elders of each temple. They ate no meat, owned little and kept peace as a vow; they taught that all life is sacred and that revenge, like a two-headed rat viper, poisons the one who takes it. Meditation filled their days, and so did play: a monk might teach a novice aim by blowing fruit pies onto his elders' heads. Each young airbender chose a sky bison as a companion for life. Villagers everywhere welcomed travelling monks for their blessings and their news. A hundred years ago the Fire Nation fell on the temples; that story is told elsewhere, and the temples stand empty.

lore.name: Air temple
lore.info: The air temples were the homes of the Air Nomads, four of them, built at the quarters of the world in places only a flyer could reach easily. The Southern Air Temple and the Northern Air Temple housed the monks, the Eastern Air Temple and the Western Air Temple the nuns. The southern temple stands on a peak in the Patola Mountain Range; the northern one on a snow-capped mountain over the Earth Kingdom's northern coast, where the bison polo championship was played; the eastern one on three mountains joined by bridges, where every young airbender chose the flying bison that would be a companion for life; the western one hangs upside down beneath a cliff edge north of the Fire Nation, its spires pointing down into the gorge, so a traveller can walk the clifftop above it and never know. Pilgrims of other nations were welcome. All four were emptied in the first days of the war. The northern temple has since been settled by Earth Kingdom refugees; the rest are left to the wind, and few dare visit them.

lore.name: Air temple sanctuaries
lore.info: At the heart of the Southern Air Temple, and of the Northern Air Temple too, lies a sanctuary, a great sealed chamber whose door has no handle and no keyhole. It answers only to airbending: a breath of air through the right pipes turns the locks with the sound of a flute. Before the war, only the Avatar and the council of elders went inside. The sanctuary of the Southern Air Temple is a tall round hall where the statues of the Avatars, one for every life the Avatar has lived, stand in a spiral that climbs toward the roof in the shape of the Air Nomad sign; the monks meditated there together, and it was held the holiest room in the temple. The monks taught that the sanctuary kept the knowledge of the Avatar and that the Avatar would meet a guide there when he was ready. Since the war no airbender has been left to open the doors, and as far as anyone knows they have stayed shut.

lore.name: Airball
lore.info: Airball was the game of the air temples. Two sides, or even two players, stood atop a forest of wooden poles of uneven height and used airbending to drive a light, slotted wooden ball from pole to pole until it passed through the spinning ring of the other side's goal. It wanted speed, balance and a good eye more than strength. Rival temples kept old grudges over it, and monks would tease one another about past defeats. The courts still stand at the temples, their poles weathered grey and their rings stuck fast. A nonbender who tries a round will find the poles very high and the ball very hard to catch.

lore.name: Airbending
lore.info: Airbending is the art of the Air Nomads, who learned it from the flying bison. It is the element of freedom and its season is autumn. An airbender does not meet force with force; they turn aside, step around, and let an attacker's own weight carry him past, so the art looks gentle until a single gust lifts a grown man off his feet. Its masters rode the wind on folding wooden gliders and could run up walls, leap from cliff to cliff and soften any fall. Airbending is the opposite of earthbending: where the earthbender roots and endures, the airbender keeps moving until the other side tires. No one has seen an airbender in a hundred years. The temples stand empty on their peaks, and children in the Earth Kingdom grow up thinking the art is a story their grandparents tell.

lore.name: Airbending training
lore.info: The monks of the four air temples trained their children young, and every one of those children could bend. The lessons taught evasion before anything else: dodging swinging sandbags, crossing ropes, balancing on posts, climbing walls without being touched. Meditation mattered as much as motion; a novice was told to let the spirit wander like the wind and that there was no wrong way to do it. Breathing kept them warm on the highest peaks. Falls were common enough that every monk knew how to set a dislocated shoulder by rubbing the muscles loose and turning the arm until the joint slid home. An airbender who mastered the art was marked with blue arrow tattoos on head, hands and feet. Those marks are the surest sign of an airbender, and no one alive has seen a fresh one inked.

lore.name: Autumnal equinox
lore.info: The autumnal equinox comes in the autumn, when the sun crosses the middle of the sky and day and night are of equal length. It is among the turning points of the year written on the sanctuary floor of the fire temple on Crescent Island, beside the two solstices. Autumn was the season of the Air Nomads, when the winds blow most often and hardest; airbenders were said to be strongest then, and more airbender children were born in autumn than in any other season. With the nomads gone, few now mark the day, though the sages still keep its place on their floor.

lore.name: Avatar
lore.info: The Avatar is the one person who can bend all four elements, the bridge between the world of people and the Spirit World, whose duty is to keep the four nations in balance. When an Avatar dies, the Avatar is born again in the next nation of the cycle: fire, then air, then water, then earth, following the seasons. Each Avatar learns the elements in that same order, starting from their own. The sages of each nation search for the newborn Avatar; the Air Nomads set out thousands of toys before their children and watched for the one who chose the four that belonged to past Avatars. The Avatar is told on their sixteenth birthday. The last Avatar anyone knew was Roku, born in the Fire Nation, and the next should have been born an Air Nomad. No Avatar has been seen in a hundred years.

lore.name: Avatar Day festival
lore.info: Every year on the anniversary of Chin's death, Chin Village holds Avatar Day, and it is no celebration of the Avatar. The village honours its founder and spends the day shaming the Avatar who, it believes, murdered him. Businesses close, stalls sell deep-fried food, candied plums and sugar dumplings on sticks, and the crowd follows a parade of giant paper effigies of past Avatars, Kyoshi and Roku among them, to the place where they are burned. The village keeps an old wheel of punishments for crimes great and small, and the charge against Kyoshi is still spoken of as an unpunished crime. A stranger who defends the Avatar aloud on that day should expect a cold reception, or a hearing before the wheel.

lore.name: Avatar relics
lore.info: When a Fire Nation Avatar died, the Air Nomads knew the next Avatar would be born among them, and the monks searched their children with the relics. Thousands of toys were laid out in a long row on faded yellow cloths, and among them were four that had belonged to Avatars past: a wooden hog monkey, a wooden hand drum, a clay turtle and a wooden whirligig. A child who passed over everything else and chose those four was thought to remember them from earlier lives. The test was trusted but not certain. The relics were kept at the air temples, and no one has seen them since the temples fell.

lore.name: Avatar State
lore.info: The Avatar holds within them the strength of every Avatar who came before. In the Avatar State that strength rises all at once: the eyes and any tattoos glow white, the voice speaks with many voices, and the Avatar bends with the power of a thousand lifetimes, moving mountains and calling up storms. It often wakes on its own when the Avatar is in mortal danger or great grief, and then the Avatar may hardly know what they have done. A fully realized Avatar can enter and leave it at will, but that takes long spiritual discipline. The state carries a danger as great as its power. The old teaching is that if the Avatar is killed while in it, the cycle of rebirth is broken and the Avatar will never return.

lore.name: Avatar Temple
lore.info: Every nation built at least one temple to the Avatar, a shrine tied to the Avatar Spirit and to every life it has lived. They are holy ground, and some nations guard them closely: only the elder monks entered the Air Nomads' sanctuary, and only Fire Sages live in the fire temple on Crescent Island, behind a sanctuary door that takes five firebenders to open. The Avatar is exempt from every such rule. The sages of these temples keep watch on statues and painted hangings of the Avatars, because it is taught that their eyes light up when the Avatar enters the Avatar State anywhere in the world. They have not lit in a hundred years. Since the Avatar vanished, the Fire Sages have pledged themselves to the Fire Lord instead, and a stranger asking at a Fire Nation temple about the Avatar is asking a dangerous question.

lore.name: Ba Sing Se University
lore.info: The greatest university in the world by its own account, in the grove district of the Middle Ring of Ba Sing Se, educating the Earth Kingdom's scholars and exchange students from the other nations, with faculties of anthropology, history and the rest and expeditions that go looking for the things the books describe. Zei, a professor of anthropology, has spent his career looking for Wan Shi Tong's Library. A stranger with a question finds a scholar; a stranger with a map finds a professor. One sworn to the university studies, copies, digs, and rises by what they bring back.

lore.name: Badgermoles and the first earthbenders
lore.info: Badgermoles are enormous blind diggers of the Earth Kingdom's mountains, brown with a white stripe between two black ones down the back and a white mask over the face. They feel the world through the earth and bend it to tunnel, and the oldest stories say people learned earthbending by watching them: the lovers Oma and Shu were taught by badgermoles. In the Kolau Mountain Range the badgermoles keep reshaping the tunnels under the mountains, so no map of the passes stays true for long. They eat worms as cubs and wolfbats as adults. They love music, which puts them into a kind of daze, and a badgermole calmed that way can be ridden or set to work. At Earth Rumble in Gaoling they clear the ring of rubble between bouts.

lore.name: Ballista
lore.info: The ballista is a giant crossbow on a turning mount, strung with twisted cord to throw darts, arrows and harpoons farther and faster than any catapult. Fire Navy ships carry it to cripple other vessels: the bolt punches through a hull below the waterline, then springs barbs so it cannot be pulled free, and the crew hauls the prey in on its chain. Fortress towers and prison walls mount the same weapon. A ballista bolt's chain is its weak point; a quick blade or a sharp jet of water can cut it before the winch takes up the slack.

lore.name: Banyan-grove tree
lore.info: At the centre of the Foggy Swamp stands the banyan-grove tree, a single tree so old and so large that the whole swamp is made of it. Its branches dropped shoots that rooted and grew into new trunks, which dropped shoots of their own, until one tree became a forest miles wide; its roots run under every channel and island in the swamp. The swamp folk say this is the lesson of the place: everything is one living thing, and people who think themselves separate are branches of the same tree. They say a waterbender of their tribe reached enlightenment sitting beneath it. Some believe that a person who lays a hand on its roots and is quiet enough can feel the whole swamp through them, and find whoever is lost in it. The Foggy Swamp Tribe guards the tree fiercely, and anyone who comes to cut or burn it will meet the swamp before they meet the tree.

lore.name: Battle of Garsai
lore.info: Garsai, a city of the western Earth Kingdom, fell to the Fire Nation in one of the early battles that won the war its foothold on the continent. The Fire Nation force was commanded by Azulon, Sozin's son and heir, and the victory made his name. He was praised across the nation for his leadership there, and when he took the throne after his father he carried that reputation into the long middle years of the war. For the Fire Nation, Garsai is a name in the schoolbooks beside Han Tui. For the western provinces it marks the years when the Earth Kingdom's armies stopped holding the coast and began to fall back.

lore.name: Battle of Han Tui
lore.info: Fire Nation schoolchildren learn Han Tui as a lesson in generalship. Early in the war Fire Lord Sozin himself led an army against the Earth Kingdom city, and his force was outnumbered. He counted his advantages instead of his soldiers: a long drought had dried the country and thinned the defenders' stores, and the city lay downwind of his camp. His firebenders set the land alight, the wind carried the blaze to the walls, and the city's defences burned to nothing in minutes. Earth Kingdom losses were terrible and the Fire Nation's were light. In the Earth Kingdom the battle is remembered less as cleverness than as the first proof of what fire does to a dry country in a hard wind.

lore.name: Battlements
lore.info: Fire Lord Sozin laid a road of switchbacks from the beach below the Fire Nation Capital up to the city and lined it with watchtowers and turrets, making it one of the most heavily fortified roads in the world. The turrets are small stone towers, each with at least two soldiers, firebenders and a chained harpoon crossbow among them, set on cliff shelves and triangular platforms above the harbour approach. They overlook the shallow, clear water of the bay, so anything that swims or sails in is seen. The road is the only way up from the shore, and strangers who walk it are watched from every bend.

lore.name: Bending arts
lore.info: Bending is the gift of moving an element with the body and the will: water, earth, fire or air, each worked through a martial style that carries the temper of its element. A bender reaches past the skin with their own chi, the energy that runs through every living thing, and the element answers. Each art belongs to a people: the Water Tribe bends water, the Earth Kingdom earth, the Fire Nation fire and the Air Nomads air, though swamp folk and desert tribes keep their own ways. The gift is not shared out evenly. Every Air Nomad was born a bender, but in the other nations most people are not, and two bending parents can raise a child who never moves a pebble. No one bends two elements except the Avatar. A stranger should know that in this war the art a person bends is the first thing a soldier reads on them, and sometimes the only thing.

lore.name: Bihou
lore.info: Bihou was a small Earth Kingdom farming village of houses built on and around a hill, joined by paths and stone steps, with fields below and woods all round. It had no garrison and no militia. In 91 AG a Fire Nation raiding band, the Rough Rhinos among them, came to take it, and the villagers refused to submit and fought back with what they had. In answer the soldiers burned the whole village to the ground and killed many of its people, parents in front of their children. The survivors fled into the woods, and some of the orphans never came out again as anything but fighters. Bihou is not rebuilt. Earth Kingdom folk of the region tell its story as a warning of what happens when a village resists, and some of the young tell it as the reason to resist.

lore.name: Bloodbending
lore.info: A few waterbenders, late at night and well away from their masters, wonder aloud about a question no school will answer. A body is mostly water; the full moon makes every waterbender stronger; so what could a strong enough bender do to a person's own blood under a full moon? Masters in the North shut such talk down at once and will not say whether they shut it down because the idea is foolish or because it is not. No one has ever been known to do it, and no tribe has a word for it that is spoken kindly. Every tribe agrees on one thing: to take hold of another person's body would be the darkest use of the art there is, and anyone who learned it would never admit to it.

lore.name: Blue jay
lore.info: The blue jay is a crested songbird, bright blue on the head, back, wings and tail, white underneath and round the eyes, and the crest rises and falls with its mood. It has learned to live alongside people and is at home among the rooftops of Ba Sing Se. It does not need people, though: a flock still lives in the ruins of Taku, where no one has lived for a long time. A jay calling over an empty town is often the only sound in it. It is one of the few birds in the world that is not some cross of two other animals.

lore.name: Boar
lore.info: The boar is a plain wild pig of the remote Earth Kingdom forests, compact on short legs with cloven hooves, a big head with a long snout and flared nostrils, small folded ears and four tusks curving up from the lower jaw. It is hunted everywhere for its meat, and a whole roast boar is the centre of any feast worth the name, at festivals and gatherings across the world. Hunters take them for the table wherever the forests are deep enough to hold them, and a festival without one is a poor festival.

lore.name: Body markings in the World of Avatar
lore.info: Marks on the skin say who a person is and what they have done. An airbending master bore five blue arrows, one from the forehead down the spine and one along each limb, earned by mastering every tier of the art. Water Tribe warriors paint their faces black, grey and white before battle, and in the North the chief marks volunteers for a dangerous mission with three red lines on the forehead. In the South a youth who comes through ice dodging is marked for what they showed: a crescent moon for bravery, an arc for trust, an arc over a dot for wisdom. Kyoshi Warriors wear white paint with red and black, after Avatar Kyoshi's own face. The Yuyan Archers bear a dark red tattoo across the eyes. Tattoos are common among pirates and criminals too, and the prisoners of Chin Village say a tattoo is the quickest way to fit in behind bars.

lore.name: Booby trap
lore.info: The Fire Navy rigs its ships against boarders and looters. A tripwire across a passage can slam doors, seal a hold and loose a signal flare into the sky, so a crew or a nearby patrol knows someone is aboard before the intruder knows he has been caught. The habit runs through the whole navy, and even a long-abandoned hulk can keep its snares working, its flare still waiting to call a ship that may be close. Anyone searching a Fire Nation vessel should walk slowly, look low and touch nothing strung across a doorway.

lore.name: Bosco
lore.info: The Earth King keeps a bear. Bosco is his pet and, by every account from inside the walls, his best friend. He roams the grounds of the Earth Kingdom Royal Palace at the king's side, sits by the throne when the king gives audience, has grown fat on cakes and pies, and is the guest of honour at birthday feasts thrown in his name. Few outside the palace have ever seen either the king or the bear; the Upper Ring hears about both only through those who serve there. Visitors lucky enough to be received should be polite to the bear, since the king trusts the bear's judgment of people.

lore.name: Bounty Hunting
lore.info: Where the law cannot reach, money does. The Fire Nation posts wanted notices with a face, a name and a reward, and deserters, rebels and enemies of the crown fill the boards in every port and colony. Earth Kingdom towns post their own for bandits and thieves. The work is taken by hunters for hire: lone trackers like June, who rides a shirshu that can follow a scent across a continent and drop its quarry with one touch of its tongue, and bands like the Rough Rhinos, who take a contract on any notorious head for the right price. A hunter is paid for the wanted, not for questions, and rarely cares whether a notice is just. Against them a fugitive's only friends are distance, a new name and towns that ask nothing.

lore.name: Buzzard wasps of the desert
lore.info: Buzzard wasps nest in caves they dig into the rock spires of the Si Wong Desert: six-legged insects the size of a dog, with a vulture's bald head and hooked beak on a striped wasp's body, and razor-sharp talons. They eat carrion, dead travellers included, and hunt the living when hungry. Prey is carried back to the hive, chewed and turned into a honey-like paste on the walls that feeds the young and tastes of rotten meat. A colony attacks together when its nest is entered or when there is loud noise. Wasps circling overhead mean something below is dying. The desert would be a fouler place without them, and that is the only good thing anyone says of them.

lore.name: Cabbage slug
lore.info: The cabbage slug is a tiny brown and white pest of the Earth Kingdom that burrows deep into a cabbage head and eats it from the inside, so the damage is seldom seen until the crop is lost. A few slugs breed fast enough to strip a whole patch in under a week. That is why the ferry terminal at Full Moon Bay refuses produce that might carry them into Ba Sing Se: inspectors split suspect cabbages, and the guards feed condemned loads to the platypus bear they keep for the purpose. A cabbage seller crossing to the city should expect to lose his cargo, and arguing will only bring the guards.

lore.name: Canyon crawlers of the Great Divide
lore.info: Canyon crawlers haunt the Great Divide and the dry country of the western Earth Kingdom: a crocodile's head with four eyes on each side and a forked tongue, a two-part body and four long spider legs that run straight up a canyon wall. Their eyes are poor but their many nostrils are keen, and the smell of food draws them from far off. They prefer live meat but will eat anything. Canyon guides forbid food on the descent for this reason, and a party that smuggles some down may be swarmed. Herbalists swear burning mint leaves hides the smell and keeps crawlers off, and some travellers carry bundles. A blow to those nostrils, or a strong gust of wind, drives one off for a while.

lore.name: Catgators of the swamp
lore.info: The catgator is the Foggy Swamp's bottom-feeder, a squat, dark-green reptile seven or eight feet long, with a ridged back, a flat head, a mouth full of teeth, catfish whiskers on its snout and a little fin at the end of its tail. It looks murderous and is in fact docile toward people. Most catgators eat anything they come across except the swamp's big insects, which keeps a camp free of pests, and so the Foggy Swamp Tribe and some Earth Kingdom folk keep them as pets and give them names. Some are picky eaters. Its teeth are a medicine ingredient. Most outsiders find it revolting, but a swamp family's catgator is family.

lore.name: Cavehopper
lore.info: Cavehoppers are blind, white insects that live their whole lives in the damp caves of the Fire Nation coast. They feel their way with long antennae and sticky, half-webbed feet that sense the smallest tremor in the rock. Sunlight burns their pale bodies, so they never leave the dark, and they never stop jumping. They eat algae and are eaten in turn by cave salamanders and by the toucan puffins that wander in from the shore. A knock on a cave wall sends a shower of them leaping. People who are hungry enough eat them too, but most spit them out.

lore.name: Chey
lore.info: Chey was a captain of the Fire Army and an explosives expert who blew up villages for the war until he could no longer stand what he saw. About three years before winter 99 AG he walked away from his unit and lived, the second man ever to do so after Jeong Jeong, and he went looking for the old master to learn what he knew. He jokes that being second earns a man no legend. The Fire Nation posts his likeness on wanted notices across the Earth Kingdom, drawn in his old uniform and marked mentally unstable. Anyone who recognises him has a choice to make: the army pays for deserters, and the deserter knows the woods where the old master hides.

lore.name: Chi
lore.info: Chi is the energy that flows through all living things, and every bending art rests on it. A bender extends their chi past the body to move an element; a healer guides it along its paths to close a wound; a chi-blocker strikes those same paths to stop it cold. Firebenders gather chi with each breath and loose it as flame. Northern healers learn the paths on a carved figure marked with every channel before they touch a patient. Teahouses and apothecaries sell brews that promise to fill a warrior with fighting energy, and most of them only set the heart racing. Swamp dwellers and hermit monks teach that all life shares the same roots, and that a person still enough can feel where someone they love has gone.

lore.name: Chi-blocking
lore.info: Chi-blocking is an old and quiet art of striking the points where chi runs close beneath the skin. A few quick jabs leave an arm limp, a leg folding, or a bender suddenly unable to call their element, for as long as it takes the flow to return. It needs no bending, only speed, flexibility and a precise knowledge of the body, and so it is a nonbender's weapon against benders. It was kept secret for centuries and most people still have never heard of it; a soldier who goes down to an unarmed acrobat is more likely to blame a cramp than an art. A stranger who sees someone fight with two fingers and never a fist should keep their distance and keep moving.

lore.name: Chin
lore.info: Chin the Conqueror is a hero in one village and a tyrant everywhere else. To the Earth Kingdom at large he is a half-remembered warlord who nearly took the whole continent and fell off a cliff. To the people of Chin Village, founded by his followers where he died, he is their great emperor, a glorious leader murdered by the Avatar. His statue stands in their square. The argument over him has run for more than three centuries and shows no sign of ending: his admirers call him a glorious leader, his critics a horrible tyrant whose own pride killed him. Travellers passing through the village do well to keep their opinion of him to themselves.

lore.name: Clam
lore.info: The clams of the Jang Hui River were once the floating village's living: dug from the riverbed, eaten at every meal and sold to boats passing down the river. Since the Fire Nation Army factory upstream began dumping its waste in the water, the clams come up brown and blistered, full of mud, weed and dead insects, and the rest of the river's catch comes up twisted and strange. The fishmongers still sell them, because there is nothing else to sell. A visitor will be offered them on every pier. A polite refusal is understood; a disgusted one is not forgiven.

lore.name: Council of Elders
lore.info: Each of the four air temples was governed by its own council of elders, senior monks or nuns who were at once the temple's rulers and its spiritual teachers. Every member was a master airbender long past earning the arrows. The councils set the rules of their temples, decided who would speak for the Air Nomads to the world, and alone besides the Avatar could enter the sanctuary at each temple's heart. They watched the young, and when the Avatar was born among the nomads, it was the elders who found and named the child. They were kind, and they could be set in their ways: when a council judged that a young Avatar should be taken from his teacher and trained elsewhere, it was not easily argued with. No council has sat for a hundred years.

lore.name: Council of Five
lore.info: The five highest generals of the Earth Kingdom's army, the highest authority in its military, who oversee the whole war from a chamber in Ba Sing Se under General How, with General Sung among them holding the Outer Wall. The council also commands the Royal Earthbender Guards. It has not seen the Earth King in years. A stranger does not meet the council; an officer of rank waits a month to. One sworn to the council serves its chamber as a runner, a clerk, an aide, a staff officer, and rises by carrying what the generals cannot be seen to carry.

lore.name: Counting the years
lore.info: The four nations count the years of this age from Sozin's Comet. The year the comet came and the war began is year nought; the years after it are numbered after the genocide of the Air Nomads, written AG, and the years before it before the genocide, written BG. Roku died in 12 BG and Kyoshi in 82 BG; Chin fell in Kyoshi's lifetime, some three hundred and seventy years before this winter. This winter is the winter of 99 AG, the last of the war's first hundred years, and the comet that began the count is due back at the end of the coming summer. Scholars still reckon the deep past by the lives of the Avatars, and common folk reckon it by what their grandparents saw.

lore.name: Courtesy in the Fire Nation
lore.info: The Fire Nation is a country of bows. One greets an elder or a superior with the fire salute: one hand held flat and upright, the other a fist beneath it, the flat hand standing for the superior and the fist for the one below. It is made on meeting and on leaving, after business and when something good has happened, and a soldier takes an order with the salute alone. Before a member of the royal family a subject goes down on his face; to stay standing is an insult that may be answered with an Agni Kai. Honour lives in the outward show, in dress, posture and hair, and in the way one speaks of the Fire Lord, whose portrait hangs in schools and public halls and whose statues stand in the squares. A stranger who learns only one Fire Nation gesture should learn the salute.

lore.name: Crossing the Si Wong Desert
lore.info: Nobody crosses the Si Wong Desert lightly. It is the largest, driest and hottest desert in the world, miles of barren sand in the middle of the Earth Kingdom, outside the reach of any government. The sandbenders sail it on wind and sand, and the beetle-headed merchants trade across it, and even they lose people to thirst and sun. The one great landmark in all that sand is a towering rock that rises alone from the dunes; travellers steer by it, but nobody camps beneath it, because a hive of buzzard wasps lives inside and will carry off anything that disturbs them. The cactus that grows in the desert holds water, but its juice clouds the mind and has driven travellers wandering in circles. The rules are simple: carry more water than you think, travel with people who know the way, and never drink from the cactus.

lore.name: Cultural Ambassadors
lore.info: The women assigned as guides to every important guest of Ba Sing Se in the late war, all called Joo Dee, all with the same calm, polished, mechanical smile, whose work is to keep outside influences from the city and the city's rule of silence from being broken. They are the first face a guest sees and the last. A stranger of rank is given one; a stranger without rank is reported by one. One sworn to the ambassadors is a smile at a guest's elbow, and rises by the Dai Li's satisfaction with how little the guest learned.

lore.name: Currency
lore.info: Money in the four nations is metal, and the metal is what it is worth: gold above silver above copper. Earth Kingdom coins are round with a square hole so they can be strung on a cord; copper, silver and gold differ in metal, and the gold has a richer rim. For great sums there are small gold ingots shaped like boats. Fire Nation coins are angular, with the national emblem on one face and writing on the other: the copper piece a rectangle with two curved sides, the silver piece a small pentagon, the gold piece long, with a slit up its middle. Water Tribe money is blue, thick and shaped like a ring, and is taken in some Earth Kingdom towns and refused in others. Omashu issues its own vouchers, good at any lawful business in the city. Merchants everywhere call any coin a piece, and weigh it if they doubt it.

lore.name: Cutter sailing ship
lore.info: The Southern Water Tribe's war boat is the cutter: a deep, curved hull with a bow that sweeps high and is roped to a single wooden mast, one or two blue triangular sails, a yellow lantern hanging from the prow and the tribe's emblem flying at the masthead. Built for the icy South, it sails well anywhere. In 97 AG Chief Hakoda took the tribe's warriors north on eight cutters to fight beside the Earth Kingdom, and their boats now harry Fire Nation shipping in the eastern seas. Southern fathers build their own cutters and take their children ice dodging in them, steering between floating bergs.

lore.name: Dai Li
lore.info: The elite secret police of Ba Sing Se, founded by Avatar Kyoshi to protect the city's cultural heritage, who capture, interrogate and imprison anyone who threatens the peace of the city as Long Feng, the city's grand secretariat, defines it. Men in green robes and conical hats with stone gloves on their hands, moving on the rooftops and in the earth. A stranger is watched from the ferry; a stranger who mentions the war is visited. One sworn to the Dai Li keeps the city's peace and the city's secrets, and rises by learning which is which.

lore.name: Dark spirits
lore.info: An angry spirit is a wronged one, the old people say: when a spirit's place is harmed or forgotten, the spirit turns on whoever lives nearby. A forest spirit whose trees are burned, a river spirit whose water is fouled, a shrine nobody tends any more: these are where the angry ones come from. Such a spirit can take a shape that blows and blades pass through, drag people off into the night, and wreck a village that never knew what it did wrong. The solstices thin the wall between the worlds, so the worst of it comes then. The remedy every elder gives is the same: find what was harmed and mend it, and do not fight what cannot be cut.

lore.name: District: Ba Sing Se
lore.info: Ba Sing Se is a district of the Four Nations. The capital of the Earth Kingdom and the last great stronghold of the war: the Outer Wall, the Agrarian Zone, the Inner Wall, and the Lower Ring, the Middle Ring and the Upper Ring inside it, the Earth Kingdom Royal Palace at the centre, Lake Laogai beside it and the monorail over all of it. The Dai Li keep the city, and the city keeps its peace by never mentioning the war. In the spring of 100 AG the drill comes to the Outer Wall and the coup follows; after it the Fire Nation holds the walls. The roads are the monorail and the ring gates. Its hub is Lower Ring; its other places: Outer Wall, Agrarian Zone, Inner Wall, Drill Site, Ba Sing Se Zoo, Middle Ring, Kuanming Square restaurant, Ba Sing Se University, Firelight Fountain, Upper Ring, Earth Kingdom Royal Palace, Jasmine Dragon, Team Avatar's Upper Ring house, Iroh and Zuko's apartment, Fancy Lady Day Spa, Lake Laogai, Ba Sing Se Prison. By land it joins The Lakes and the Serpent's Pass, The Northern Mountains.

lore.name: District: Capital Island
lore.info: Capital Island is a district of the Four Nations. The largest island of the Fire Nation and the seat of its power: the Fire Nation Capital sits inside a volcanic crater behind the Great Gates of Azulon, with the Fire Nation Royal Palace, the Royal Plaza and the Capital City Prison in its heart. Fire Lord Ozai rules from here from 95 AG, and the Fire Army, the Fire Navy and the Domestic Forces answer to him. A stranger needs papers, a reason and a straight back; a foreigner needs more. The roads are the harbour steps and the plaza avenues, and the only way off the island is by sea. Its hub is Fire Nation Capital; its other places: Fire Nation Royal Palace, High Temple, Royal Plaza, Capital City Prison, Mai's house, Great Gates of Azulon, Harbour Quarter, Crater Rim Batteries, Noble Hill, Capital Drill Ground, Ash Market, Royal Palace gardens, Royal spa. By land it joins nothing; by sea The Fire Islands (across the Fire Nation's home waters).

lore.name: District: Kolau and the South-West
lore.info: Kolau and the South-West is a district of the Four Nations. The Kolau Mountain Range and the land it shelters: Omashu on its peak with its delivery system and its mad king, the Cave of Two Lovers under the pass, the Foggy Swamp and the Foggy Swamp Tribe, Ketu Harbor, and the plains village and Tu Zin on the dry country to the east. Omashu holds free until the spring of 100 AG, when it surrenders and becomes New Ozai. The roads climb and the mountain passes decide who gets through. Its hub is Omashu; its other places: Omashu Royal Palace, Cave of Two Lovers, Foggy Swamp, Foggy Swamp Tribe, Ketu Harbor, Tu Zin, Plains village, Lee Family Pig Farm, Farming village, Farming village hospital, Kolau Mountain Range, Kolau Pass. By land it joins Si Wong and the Plains, The Mo Ce Coast, The Southern Coast.

lore.name: District: Si Wong and the Plains
lore.info: Si Wong and the Plains is a district of the Four Nations. The Si Wong Desert at the heart of the continent, the largest and driest in the world, and the rocky plains around it: the Misty Palms Oasis on its south-west edge, Wan Shi Tong's Library buried in the sand, the Great Divide to the north-west, the Si Wong tribes' camps and the beetle-headed merchants' routes. Nobody rules the desert; the Earth Kingdom stops at its edge. The roads are sand-sailer tracks and caravan trails, and the sun is the first enemy. Its hub is Misty Palms Oasis; its other places: Flower shop, Wan Shi Tong's Library, Great Divide, Waterfall pond, Si Wong Desert, Sandbender Camp, Beetle-Head Caravanserai, Gan Jin Camp, Zhang Camp. By land it joins Kolau and the South-West, The Lakes and the Serpent's Pass, The Northern Mountains, The Southern Coast.

lore.name: District: The Lakes and the Serpent's Pass
lore.info: The Lakes and the Serpent's Pass is a district of the Four Nations. The East and West Lakes south-west of Ba Sing Se, divided by the pinnacles of the Serpent's Pass, and Full Moon Bay on the eastern lake where the hidden ferry station takes refugees across to the city. Every refugee from the south comes through here with a passport or a bribe, and those without take the Serpent's Pass on foot. The ferry is the road; the Serpent's Pass is the other road. Its hub is Full Moon Bay; its other places: Serpent's Pass, East and West Lakes, Pass Southern Gate, Pass Northern Gate, Drowned Road, West Lake Fishing Village, Lakeshore Camp. By land it joins Ba Sing Se, Si Wong and the Plains.

lore.name: District: The Mo Ce Coast
lore.info: The Mo Ce Coast is a district of the Four Nations. The Earth Kingdom's western shore on the Mo Ce Sea: forest and river country with the river village at the forks, Senlin Village, Gaipan and the Freedom Fighters' trees, Taku's ruins, Makapu Village under its volcano, the Abbey, General Fong's fortress and the Pohuai Stronghold where the Yuyan Archers keep the Fire Nation colonies' northern edge. The war has been here longest: burned forest, occupied villages, a prison rig offshore. The roads are old and watched, and the coast is where pirates and smugglers sell what the armies lose. Its hub is River village; its other places: Gaipan, Taku, Pohuai Stronghold, Mining village, Seaport village, General Fong's fortress, Garsai, Senlin Village, Scorched forest, Makapu Village, Mt. Makapu, Abbey, Harbor town, Roadside kiosk, Tavern, Prison rig, Fire Nation colonial village, Village resort, Seedy merchants pier, Waterfall lagoon. By land it joins Kolau and the South-West, The Northern Mountains; by sea The Fire Islands (across the Mo Ce Sea), The Northern Water Tribe (across the Northern Sea).

lore.name: District: The Northern Mountains
lore.info: The Northern Mountains is a district of the Four Nations. The Taihua Mountains along the continent's north, from the Northern Air Temple and the mechanist's colony down to Han Tui and Chameleon Bay, where the Southern Water Tribe's men hold an inlet against the Fire Navy. The temple's gliders and machines are the war's newest things; the mountains are the war's oldest ground. The roads are high, cold and few. Its hub is Northern Air Temple; its other places: Taihua Mountains, Han Tui, Chameleon Bay, Taihua High Road, Northern Coast Watchtower, Mountain Hermitage. By land it joins Ba Sing Se, Si Wong and the Plains, The Mo Ce Coast; by sea The Northern Water Tribe (across the Northern Sea).

lore.name: District: The Northern Water Tribe
lore.info: The Northern Water Tribe is a district of the Four Nations. The North Pole and the ice city of Agna Qel'a, Chief Arnook's seat, with the Northern Water Tribe Royal Palace, the canals, the great sea wall and the Spirit Oasis hidden at its heart where Tui and La swim. The North has never fallen and has not fought in a hundred years, until the Siege of the North in the winter of 100 AG. Master Pakku teaches the men to fight and the women to heal. The roads are canals and the sea gate. Its hub is Agna Qel'a; its other places: Northern Water Tribe Royal Palace, North Pole Tundra, Sea Wall, Healers' Hut, Canal Market, Northern Fishing Grounds. By land it joins nothing; by sea The Mo Ce Coast (across the Northern Sea), The Northern Mountains (across the Northern Sea), The Spirit World (across the Spirit Oasis's far side).

lore.name: District: The South
lore.info: The South is a district of the Four Nations. The Southern Archipelago and the South Pole continent: the Southern Air Temple on its peak in the Patola Mountain Range, Whaletail Island, and the Southern Water Tribe's village at Wolf Cove, stripped of its waterbenders by the raids and of its men by the war. Hakoda's warriors left in 97 AG; Kanna, Katara and Sokka and the children and old people remain. There are no roads, only the ice, the cutters and the sea. Its hub is Wolf Cove; its other places: Southern Air Temple, Patola Mountain Range, Whaletail Island, Shipwreck, South Pole Ice, Iceberg Field, Penguin Slopes, Old Southern Harbour. By land it joins nothing; by sea The Southern Coast (across the South Sea).

lore.name: District: The Southern Coast
lore.info: The Southern Coast is a district of the Four Nations. The Earth Kingdom's south coast along the Nan Shan River and the South Sea: Gaoling with Earth Rumble and the Beifong Estate Chin Village and its prison, Kyoshi Island with Suki's village and the Kyoshi Warriors, the quarry campsite, and the Eastern Air Temple as the far place to the south-east. The war has not reached these towns, which is why they pretend it is not happening. The roads are country roads; the sea road runs to the Southern Water Tribe. Its hub is Gaoling; its other places: Master Yu's Earthbending Academy, Chin Village, Chin Village prison, Kyoshi Island, Suki's village, Kyoshi Shrine, Kyoshi Landing, Quarry campsite, Nan Shan River, Eastern Air Temple, Coast Road Waystation. By land it joins Kolau and the South-West, Si Wong and the Plains; by sea The South (across the South Sea).

lore.name: District: The Spirit World
lore.info: The Spirit World is a district of the Four Nations. The plane beside the world where the spirits live: the Realm of Koh, the far side of the Spirit Oasis, the spirit side of Wan Shi Tong's Library. It is reached by meditation, a solstice, or a spirit's carrying, never by road, and no bending works there unless the body comes too. Koh steals faces, Hei Bai rages for a forest, and the Avatar's past lives wait to be asked. Its hub is Spirit Oasis; its other places: Realm of Koh, Spirit Library, Spirit Woods, Hei Bai's Grove, Fog Marsh, Spirit Roads. By land it joins nothing; by sea The Northern Water Tribe (across the Spirit Oasis's far side).

lore.name: Domestic Forces
lore.info: The Fire Nation's law and home guard: the police of its cities and islands, the keepers of its prisons from the Capital City Prison to the Boiling Rock, the last line against an invasion and the trainers of the army's recruits. Its officers are mostly women, and they are the ones who read a stranger's papers, post the wanted notices and take a deserter away. A stranger is checked, filed and watched; a foreigner is checked twice. One sworn to the Domestic Forces keeps the Fire Lord's peace at home, guards what the war has taken, and rises by being the officer nobody gets past.

lore.name: Dragon Hunts
lore.info: Dragons were the first firebenders, and the Fire Nation once revered them. Fire Lord Sozin changed that. He began the custom of hunting dragons for glory: anyone who slew one earned the honorary title of Dragon, and it was said his firebending would become legendary. Nobles took to the sport eagerly, the hunts grew fiercer once the war began, and they went on through Azulon's reign until the dragons were gone. The last great dragon is said to have fallen to Iroh, Azulon's eldest son, which is one reason he is called the Dragon of the West. Spiritual leaders objected to the killing of the original firebenders and were ignored. In the same century the Fire Nation's firebending has turned harsh and aggressive, a fire fed by anger, and few of its masters still teach it as the energy of life.

lore.name: Dragonfly
lore.info: The Earth Kingdom's dragonfly is not an insect but a slender green lizard on long clawed legs, with two pairs of thin membranous wings along its back, a hooked beak, yellow eyes and three spines behind the head. Wild ones live in the warmer parts of the kingdom, but they are kept as pets everywhere. They eat insects, fish and small rodents, so a household dragonfly keeps the rats down. They are not dangerous to people, only a nuisance when loose. A strong gust knocks them about in the air, and caged too tightly they turn dull and listless. The zoo in Ba Sing Se keeps a small cage of them.

lore.name: Duels (294 - 82 BG)
lore.info: The people of Kyoshi Island tell the Avatar's meeting with Chin as a duel, and they tell it with some relish. Chin came to the neck of the peninsula in full armour at the head of his army and took a fighting stance before the Avatar. Kyoshi answered with a single blast of air that stripped him of armour and robes alike and left the conqueror standing in his underclothes in front of his own soldiers. He held his ground anyway. Only then did she split the land, and the rest of the tale belongs to the cliff. Islanders tell it as proof that their Avatar gave the conqueror every chance to walk away. In Chin Village the same duel is told as a murder, and a stranger who laughs at it there will regret it.

lore.name: Duels (65 BG - Winter 100 AG)
lore.info: One duel of recent years is told in every Fire Nation barracks: the crown prince's shame. A few years ago Ozai's son, a boy of thirteen, spoke out in a war meeting against a general's plan to spend a division of raw recruits as bait. An insult given in the Fire Lord's chamber is answered by the Fire Lord himself, so the boy was made to face his father in an Agni Kai. He refused to fight, was burned across the face, and was banished until he should bring back the Avatar. Older duels are remembered at court in quieter voices, and the court prefers them that way. The lesson every officer draws is to speak carefully in the war room.

lore.name: Earth Kingdom
lore.info: The Earth Kingdom is the largest nation in the world and the most populous, spanning most of the Great Continent and a scatter of islands off its coasts. It is ruled from Ba Sing Se by the Earth King, though his word grows thinner the farther a town lies from the capital's walls: Omashu has its own king, the desert tribes answer to nobody, and many provinces keep their own customs, dialects and laws. Most of the world's earthbenders are born here. Its people are called diverse and strong, persistent and enduring, and the century of war has tested every word. The kingdom has fallen behind the Fire Nation in machines and ships, and the war has stripped its western coast into colonies and filled its roads with refugees, yet Ba Sing Se has never fallen and the country has never stopped fighting. A stranger who speaks of the war as lost will find that people here do not like to hear it.

lore.name: Earth Kingdom ferry
lore.info: From a hidden, guarded port in Full Moon Bay, paddle-wheel ferries carry refugees across the water toward Ba Sing Se, a crossing of about one day. The boats are plain: a broad hull, a single wheel, passenger quarters below and a captain's deck above. Passage needs a ticket and a passport, and the clerks at the bay check both, because the city fears spies among the poor. The food below decks is spoiled produce and stale bread while the crew eats well on the upper deck; refugees grumble about it every crossing. Tickets are scarce, so they are stolen, forged and fought over at the bay, and a family without them has no road east but the dangerous one.

lore.name: Earth Monarch
lore.info: The Earth King rules from his palace at the heart of Ba Sing Se and by custom almost never leaves the city. Some of his subjects revere him as a god. In truth the throne's reach has always been short: the Earth Kingdom is too large for one court, and kings have long left local rulers such as the kings of Omashu in power so long as they stayed loyal. The kingdom has lived through warlords and civil wars, and Chin once took everything but the capital itself. The present Earth King, Kuei, came to the throne young and is rarely seen; outside the walls it is commonly said that the Grand Secretariat and the city's officials govern in his name. Beyond Ba Sing Se, provincial lords fight the Fire Nation with their own armies and keep their own laws.

lore.name: Earth Rumble
lore.info: The underground earthbending tournament in a giant earthen arena in Gaoling, a popular show whose front rows are destroyed by flying rocks every night, hosted and promoted by Xin Fu, with the Boulder and his rivals on the bill and a champion nobody can beat. It is a business and a fight club and a family. A stranger buys a seat; a stranger with money gets a bout. One sworn to Earth Rumble fights in the ring under a name, takes the purse or the dirt, and rises by the crowd, which is the only judge.

lore.name: Earthbender rebellions
lore.info: Wherever the Fire Nation rules Earth Kingdom land, someone fights it. The rebels are mostly farmers, villagers and orphans rather than earthbenders, armed with whatever they can hide, and they have risen in one province or another since Azulon's reign; at least once an uprising swept through several colonies before the Fire Army put it down. Omashu has long sent weapons to resistance bands across the west, though every year the Fire Nation's advance makes its supply roads harder to keep open. Some Earth Kingdom soldiers and townsfolk work for the occupiers and inform on their neighbours for pay or favour, so rebel bands are slow to trust a stranger. In occupied country, being caught earthbending where a soldier can see is reason enough for arrest.

lore.name: Earthbending
lore.info: Earthbending is the art of the Earth Kingdom, and its first masters were the badgermoles, blind diggers who shaped tunnels under the mountains. Earth is the element of substance and its season is spring. The earthbender stands their ground, takes the blow, and waits for the moment to answer, a patience the masters call neutral jing: listening, seeming to do nothing, then striking all at once. The art is as strong in defence as in attack. Earthbenders raise walls, open roads through cliffs, hurl boulders and sink a foe to the knees in stone. Its weakness is ground it cannot touch: a bender on a ship's deck or a wooden floor is cut off from the source. The Fire Nation knows it, and builds its prisons for earthbenders out of metal and out at sea.

lore.name: Earthbending ball
lore.info: In the alleys of Ba Sing Se's Lower Ring, and in Earth Kingdom villages wherever children bend, boys and girls play earthbending ball. Each side guides a leather ball across the ground with their bending, lifting the earth beneath it, and tries to drive it into the other side's goal. There is little running and less touching of the ball; the game is all stance, rooting and timing, and good players barely move their feet. It is no official sport. It is mostly a way for young benders to practise without a master watching, and it ends, more often than not, with a broken window and a shouting neighbour.

lore.name: Earthbending training
lore.info: Earthbending masters are hard, and they expect a pupil to be harder. The first lesson is rooting: stand like a tree, joined to the ground below while the branches move. Breathing and stance come before any stone is lifted. Students punch sacks of heavy sand until the knuckles learn what earth feels like, carry boulders through mazes to stay grounded, and spar on packed dirt where a lost footing means a lost bout. The deeper teachers make a student wait and listen, with eyes closed and bare feet, before striking at all. The Earth Kingdom keeps academies in its towns and drills its soldiers in squads that move as one. A visiting bender who will not take off their shoes in a good school is told politely to find another.

lore.name: Eastern Sea
lore.info: The Eastern Sea runs from the east coast of the Great Continent down to the north-eastern shores of the South Pole, dotted with islands, among them the archipelago of the Eastern Air Temple, and joined to the East and West Lakes by a narrow channel. The fishing and trading villages along it live on what the water gives them and have never been rich. In the war it is a front line: Fire Nation ships probe it again and again for a way up to Ba Sing Se by water, and Earth Kingdom forces and their allies try to keep them out. Warriors of the Southern Water Tribe sailed north to fight in these waters, and the Fire Navy has learned to fear their tangle mines, floating hide shells of seaweed and skunk fish that foul a warship's propeller. A captain in these waters keeps a lookout night and day.

lore.name: Eel hounds and their riders
lore.info: The eel hound is a long, dark-green beast, half greyhound and half eel, taller than a man and as long as a boat, with a deep chest, long legs, a slender snout and an eel's long neck and tail. Those who have ridden one say nothing runs faster over land or swims quicker. The animal is wild by nature and very hard to train, so few people try, and a trained eel hound is rare and worth a great deal. Darker green above and pale below, it is as much at home in water as on land, so a rider never has to look for a ford. Once broken it turns calm and will carry riders across rivers and bays without slowing.

lore.name: Elephant rat
lore.info: The elephant rat lives everywhere people store food: a small grey or black rodent with a pink tail, pale rings round its eyes and a long trunk for a nose, which it pokes into sacks and cracks. It rears up on its hind legs to hold its food in its forepaws. Grain merchants hate them, cooks set traps for them and most people believe they carry disease, so a kitchen with elephant rats in it is one to avoid. They are clever, though. Treated kindly they tame easily, learn tricks and even bring small gifts, usually string or rubbish, to those who feed them. In hard times the hungry cook and eat them, and some people keep a tame one as a pet.

lore.name: Ember Island Players
lore.info: The acting troupe of the Ember Island Theater, the island's only playhouse, who have no reputation for quality and take themselves entirely seriously, and who pack the house every night with the Fire Nation's best people. They stage the war as the Fire Nation would like it, and in the summer of 100 AG they put on a play about the Avatar that the Avatar himself sits through. A stranger buys a ticket; a foreigner buys one and keeps quiet. One sworn to the troupe carries a spear in the back row, learns the lines, and rises by being given a face the audience will remember.

lore.name: Empire-class battleship
lore.info: Rarer than the cruiser and twice its length, breadth and height, the Empire-class battleship is the flagship of a Fire Navy fleet. It carries three funnels, a towering conning tower ringed by extra decks, and a gilded rostrum at the prow that marks it as a royal-pattern vessel. Its crew runs to the thousands, and a fleet admiral flies a grander flag from it than any cruiser may. A battleship in a harbour means an admiral is near and something large is being planned. Sailors of the other nations count the funnels before anything else: two is a patrol, three is an armada.

lore.name: Energybending
lore.info: Before the Avatar, before the four nations, the oldest tales say people bent not the elements but the energy within themselves. Those tales tie this to the lion turtles, vast and ancient creatures with forests on their shells, which sailors swear they have anchored beside and never found again. Some sages say the lion turtles are all gone, and others that they were never more than a story. Of the art itself nothing is taught, nothing is written that anyone has found, and no living bender knows a single form of it. The tale is told as a warning more than a promise: whatever a bender's spirit can touch in another, it can be touched by in turn.

lore.name: Era of Kyoshi
lore.info: Kyoshi was the Earth Kingdom Avatar who came after Kuruk, and the world remembers her as the sternest of the Avatars. She was born on a peninsula of the southern Earth Kingdom, and when the warlord Chin came to take it she broke it from the mainland; the land became Kyoshi Island, and its people still keep her shrine. She trained the islanders in her own way of fighting, with fan, armour and painted face, and the Kyoshi Warriors keep it today. In Ba Sing Se she founded the Dai Li to guard the city's cultural heritage. Her era ended in 82 BG, when she died and the Avatar was born again in the Fire Nation as Roku. Earth Kingdom folk speak of her as proof that an Avatar can stop a tyrant; in Chin Village they speak of her as a murderer.

lore.name: Fang
lore.info: Fang was Avatar Roku's red dragon. Roku found him as an egg with no parents to guard it and raised him himself, and the two were never apart afterward. Fang grew large enough to carry the Avatar wherever he was needed, and the pair are said to have found the first Fire Nation colonies in the Earth Kingdom from the air. He lived in a cave behind Roku's cottage on his island. When the volcano erupted, the dragon would not leave his master, and the two died together under the ash. People who tell the story of Roku's death in the Fire Nation still tell it with the dragon in it, curled around the Avatar at the end.

lore.name: Fashion in the World of Avatar
lore.info: Every nation dresses in the colour of its element. The Air Nomads wore saffron, orange and brown; the Water Tribes wear blue, purple and white over furs; the Earth Kingdom wears greens, browns and gold; the Fire Nation wears red with black and gold. Within a nation, cloth shows rank. In Ba Sing Se the Lower Ring wears dark, worn browns, the Middle Ring lighter greens, and the Upper Ring pale green robes worked with gold, with fans, parasols and great hairpieces for the women. Fire Nation nobles wear round shoulder mantles that give their clothes a spiked look, while the poor of Jang Hui wear what years of river work have left them. The people of Kyoshi Island wear blue though they are Earth Kingdom folk. A traveller who wants to pass unnoticed changes colour first: a blue coat in the Fire Nation is seen before the face above it.

lore.name: Fauna in the World of Avatar
lore.info: Almost every animal in the world is two animals in one: the ostrich horse, the turtle duck, the platypus bear, the badgermole. Plain beasts that are only one thing, like the wolf or the blue jay, are rare enough to remark on. Every country has its own. The Foggy Swamp is crowded with possum chickens, swamp fireflies, elbow leeches, screeching dodos and catgators. The Great Divide has canyon crawlers. The poles have otter penguins, tiger seals, polar dogs and buffalo yaks. In the Si Wong Desert there are gilacorns, buzzard wasps, giant rhinoceros beetles that sandbenders ride, scorpions and jackalopes. A traveller who learns the animals of a country learns half of what he needs to survive it.

lore.name: Festivals of the Fire Nation
lore.info: The Fire Nation brings its festivals wherever its people live. The travelling fire festival, the Fire Days Festival, tours the colonies and occupied towns of the Earth Kingdom, staying a few weeks in each, for soldiers on leave and colonists far from home. Its crowds wear hand-carved wooden masks, merchants sell trinkets and spicy snacks, and the attractions are fireworks, firebending jugglers and magicians, displays of bending and a puppet show in which the Fire Lord is always the hero. Every festival is also a lesson in loyalty, and children learn it with their sweets. A stranger who wants to move unseen in an occupied town can do worse than buy a mask on a festival night, though the guards know that trick as well as anyone.

lore.name: Fire Army
lore.info: The land arm of the military of the Fire Nation, the most powerful army in the world, a standing force loyal to the Fire Lord that overran most of the Earth Kingdom in a hundred years of war. Its regiments hold the colonies, its tanks and komodo rhinos lead its charges, its firebenders break walls and its conscripts fill the gaps. It drills on the crater floor of the capital and ships out from its harbour. A stranger is a recruit, a prisoner or a problem; a foreigner is a prisoner. One sworn to the Fire Army marches where it is sent, holds what it takes, and rises by holding it when the Earth Kingdom tries to take it back.

lore.name: Fire Islands
lore.info: The Fire Islands are the archipelago that makes up the Fire Nation, a great many islands from Capital Island itself down to rocks too small for any map. Many carry live volcanoes, and the climate runs from mild in the north to tropical in the south. The volcanic soil is rich: farms in the lowlands grow great surpluses of rice and fruit, and the ground holds metal enough that the islanders are famous smiths. Gas seeps from the earth in places like Fire Fountain City. The same mountains that feed the islands can end them; an eruption swallowed Roku's island and the Avatar with it, and islanders still watch their peaks for smoke. By the late war the islands burn coal and oil for their factories, and their own wealth is no longer enough for what the nation wants, which is one reason the war goes on. Most people live on the coasts, close to the sea and the fishing.

lore.name: Fire Lord
lore.info: The Fire Lord rules the Fire Nation from the Fire Nation Royal Palace in the capital, and in this century the throne's word is law without appeal. It was not always so. The first Fire Lords stood at the head of the Fire Sages as much as of the state, and for long ages they shared power with sages and noble houses; over centuries the throne took that power for itself, and by Sozin's reign the Fire Lord was master of everything. Sozin, Azulon and Ozai have each directed the war in person, bent over maps with their generals. The crown passes to the eldest child unless the ruler names another heir, and rival claimants have settled their quarrel by Agni Kai. A Fire Lord is expected to be a firebender, and no subject who values his freedom criticises one aloud.

lore.name: Fire Nation
lore.info: The Fire Nation is an absolute monarchy under the Fire Lord, home to most of the world's firebenders, its islands strung along the equator in the west with the Fire Nation Capital at their centre. It has the strongest economy in the world, the largest navy, and the forges and factories that build both. Its people are taught that they have desire and will and the drive to achieve what they want, and that the war is a gift: Fire Lord Sozin told them their prosperity was meant to be shared with the rest of the world, and the schools still teach it that way. Children pledge to the Fire Lord in class. Foreign things, foreign dress and foreign talk are viewed with suspicion, and a stranger who praises the Earth Kingdom aloud can expect a visit from the authorities. The nation is proud, orderly and loyal, and very few of its citizens have ever seen the war they are winning.

lore.name: Fire Nation air force
lore.info: The air arm of the military of the Fire Nation, the newest and smallest: the war balloons the mechanist's designs gave it, and in the last summer of the war the airships, built in secret for the comet. Its crews are picked firebenders and engineers who answer to the war minister and the Fire Lord. It was born at the Northern Air Temple, where the mechanist built the first war balloon, and flies from there and from the capital's drill ground. A stranger is kept away from the balloons; a foreigner is kept further. One sworn to the air force flies, keeps the burners and the secrets, and rises by being trusted with the ships the comet is for.

lore.name: Fire Nation circus
lore.info: A travelling circus of the Fire Nation and its colonies: rope walkers, acrobats, plate jugglers, a ring master and a collection of rare animals from a lion vulture to a platypus bear, entertaining Fire Nation and Earth Kingdom families alike wherever the tents go up. Ty Lee ran away to it. A stranger buys a ticket; a stranger who can walk a rope is hired. One sworn to the circus performs, feeds the animals and moves the tents, and rises by the act the crowd remembers.

lore.name: Fire Nation colonies
lore.info: The Fire Nation's continental empire: the Earth Kingdom and old Air Nomad territories it has taken over a hundred years, governed by Fire Nation governors over a mixed people of settlers and the conquered, from the Fire Nation colonial village and Garsai and Han Tui to the coaling ports of the Mo Ce coast. Trade between the colonies and the homeland feeds the war and the governors' purses. A stranger is a settler, a subject or a suspect, by accent; a foreigner is a subject. One sworn to the colonies serves a governor's house: a clerk, a garrison officer, a tax farmer, a magistrate, and rises by keeping a colony quiet and its tribute full.

lore.name: Fire Nation cruiser
lore.info: The steel cruiser is the workhorse of the Fire Navy and the most powerful warship any nation has put on the water. It burns coal, trails black smoke from two funnels and carries a catapult or trebuchet on its deck, with enough soldiers below to put a landing party ashore. The oldest pattern was already sailing when the Hundred Year War began; one of those early ships still lies frozen in the southern ice where waterbenders stopped it during the raids. Cruisers patrol the Mo Ce Sea, the lakes of the western Earth Kingdom and the waters off Full Moon Bay, and a commander with enough of them can close a whole strait. A small boat that meets one at sea should show its papers, lower its sail and pray; no fishing skiff outruns a cruiser on a calm day.

lore.name: Fire Nation Royal Family
lore.info: The ruling family of the Fire Nation, which has held the throne for centuries through feuds, marriages and the struggle for absolute power. Fire Lord Ozai rules from the Fire Nation Royal Palace; Azula is his heir in all but name, Zuko his banished son, Iroh his brother who gave up a siege and a claim. The family is served by the Royal Procession, flattered by the nobles and feared by everyone else. A stranger meets it only as a petitioner, a prisoner or a spectacle at a rally, and a foreigner meets it as a prisoner. One sworn to the family serves its household: a page, a courier, a guard, a tutor, a spy, and rises by being useful and never, ever seen to want more.

lore.name: Fire Nation trap
lore.info: Forged of metal and sprung by weight, the Fire Nation trap is the soldier's version of the hunter's rope snare. When something steps into it, the jaws lock into a cage and a spring yanks it high into the branches, where it hangs out of reach. It can only be opened by unlatching it from outside, so whatever is caught stays caught until the trapper comes. Patrols bait them with berries or lychee nuts and hide them under twigs and leaves along forest paths, and they take animals and people alike. In the occupied woods of the Earth Kingdom, a cage hanging in a tree is a warning that a Fire Nation camp is close.

lore.name: Fire Nation trebuchet
lore.info: The trebuchet is the scourge of the world's city walls. The Fire Nation builds them in every size, from great engines bolted to the decks of the newest warships to light pieces that ride with cavalry or are dragged along by infantry. Muscled crews wind them and load flaming shot that carries farther than any bow. Older cruisers still mount the catapult; the trebuchet is the later, better weapon. The Fire Army battered the Outer Wall of Ba Sing Se with them through the long siege. A town that sees the crews assembling the beams has a day, perhaps two, before the fire starts falling.

lore.name: Fire Navy
lore.info: The sea arm of the military of the Fire Nation, the fleet that joins an archipelago into a nation and carries its war to every other shore: iron cruisers, catapults, the blockades that keep the Earth Kingdom's coast and the North's sea, and the armada that gathers for the comet. Its ships coal at the seaport village and the Fire Nation's home harbours, and its admirals answer to the Fire Lord alone. A stranger on a Fire Navy deck is cargo; a foreigner is a prisoner. One sworn to the Fire Navy sails where it is sent, keeps the blockade, and rises by taking what the sea gives: a prize, a port, an Avatar.

lore.name: Fire Navy communication towers
lore.info: Since the start of the war, Fire Navy engineers have raised dozens of tall towers out of the sea, each one a post that keeps the navy's ships and fleets in touch across the world. The messages travel by dragon hawk: the towers house the birds, give them a place to land, and keep intelligence officers on watch to read and send what they carry. Commanders meet in them to make plans and send their orders out. Every tower must know where every ship of the fleet is deployed, and its records list each one's last reported position, which makes the towers among the most guarded places in the navy and the richest prize an enemy spy could reach. A ship that loses touch with its tower is presumed sunk.

lore.name: Fire Sages
lore.info: The religious authority of the Fire Nation, the keepers of its temples from the High Temple in the capital to the Crescent Island Fire Temple, who crown and bury the Fire Lords, marry the royal family, and find the Avatar when he is born in the Fire Nation. They once served the Avatar; for a hundred years they have served the Fire Lord. A stranger is given a blessing and a lecture; a foreigner is given the lecture. One sworn to the Fire Sages tends a temple's flame, keeps its records, and rises by learning what the records say and when to keep silent.

lore.name: Firebending
lore.info: Firebending is the art of the Fire Nation, the element of power, and its season is summer. Alone of the four, it does not need its element nearby: the firebender makes flame from their own breath and inner heat, and can also seize a fire already burning. The art draws strength from the sun, peaks at noon, and burns hottest of all when the great comet passes, as it did in the year Fire Lord Sozin began the war. Its forms are direct and relentless, a volley of strikes that leaves the foe no room to breathe. Old scholars say the first firebenders learned from the dragons, though the dragons were hunted for glory until none were left. In the Fire Nation today most teachers tell their students that rage is the fuel, and the flames that come out of a Fire Army drill yard are angry ones.

lore.name: Firebending training
lore.info: Fire Nation teachers say the power of fire comes from the breath and not the muscles, and students spend hours on breathing before they are allowed a spark: in through the nose, slowly out through the mouth. A favourite drill is to sit before a row of candles and make the flames rise and fall with each breath. Firm stances follow, and strikes from them, drilled until every movement is exact, because a firebender's precision is the measure of their fire. Self-control is the first and hardest lesson; fire is alive, it grows, and a careless student burns more than the target. Schools and military academies across the Fire Nation turn out young benders by the hundred. Most are taught that drive and anger are what keep the flame lit.

lore.name: Firefly
lore.info: Ordinary fireflies, with slender antennae and a soft green or blue glow in the tail, live in many parts of the Earth Kingdom and are one of the few creatures still found in the Northern Air Temple. The settlers who live there now use them in lanterns. Parts of the mountain leak a gas that blows up at a naked flame, and after one such blast taught them the hard way, the Mechanist's people light their deep passages only with jars of fireflies, a light source that cannot burn. It is a dim light, barely enough to see a step by, but a guest should carry nothing else into those passages.

lore.name: Five-Seven-Five Society
lore.info: A society of young women of Ba Sing Se's richest families who practise the art of traditional haiku under a strict madame, with poetry meetings, tea parties, garden parties and a guard who throws out anyone unworthy of the art. A line with a syllable too many is a disgrace. A stranger is admitted if invited and expelled on the first bad line; a stranger who counts well may stay. One sworn to the society composes, recites and judges, and rises by the madame's silence, which is praise.

lore.name: Flying boar
lore.info: The flying boar is a pale boar with great white feathered wings. It is rarely seen anywhere but in pictures, most famously as the emblem of the Beifong family of Gaoling, which carries a winged boar on its gates, banners and sedan chairs. Animal handlers in a few places have tamed living ones and ride them as mounts, and anyone who has seen it done tells the story for years. For most Earth Kingdom people the flying boar means Beifong money, and a carriage with the winged boar on it is one the road makes way for.

lore.name: Foggy Swamp Tribe
lore.info: The third of the Water Tribes, descended from southerners who settled the Foggy Swamp long ago and bend the water in its vines and fog in a way neither pole would recognise, living in stilt huts in leaf skirts, eating possum chicken and believing the whole swamp is one tree. Huu guards it as a swamp monster. A stranger is fed and shown the banyan; a stranger who harms the swamp meets the monster. One sworn to the tribe learns the vines, the fog and the tree, and rises by understanding what the tree shows.

lore.name: Four nations
lore.info: The world is divided into four nations: the Water Tribe, the Earth Kingdom, the Fire Nation and the Air Nomads, each tied to one element and one bending art. The old belief holds that balance among them keeps the world in balance, and that one nation grown too strong or brought too low throws everything into disorder. A common saying runs through all four: fire is the element of power, its people full of desire and will; earth is the element of substance, its people diverse, persistent and enduring; air is the element of freedom, its people detached from worldly concerns; water is the element of change, its people adaptable and bound by a deep sense of community. The Avatar alone bends all four and is born into each nation in turn. For a hundred years the balance has been broken.

lore.name: Fox antelope
lore.info: Herds of fox antelope graze the open grassland of the Agrarian Zone of Ba Sing Se, between the Outer Wall and the Inner Wall. Each has the spiral horns and slender legs of an antelope on a fox's body: rust-red above, white at the belly, round the eyes and at the tip of a bushy tail. They eat prairie grass and other low plants. Farmers in the zone treat them as part of the landscape. Refugees who come in through the Outer Wall and see them leaping in the evening light often take them as the first proof that the city really does hold whole countrysides inside its stone.

lore.name: Freedom Fighters
lore.info: A band of Earth Kingdom refugee teenagers and children under Jet, fighting the Fire Nation from a treetop hideout near Gaipan with hook swords, traps and ambushes, meaning to rid the world of firebenders whatever it costs the people in the way. They steal from the occupiers and feed the occupied, and they are children. A stranger is tested and recruited or tied up; a Fire Nation stranger is a target. One sworn to the Freedom Fighters lives in the trees, fights the way Jet fights, and rises by Jet's regard, which is quick to give and quick to take back.

lore.name: Gan Jin
lore.info: A tribe of the northern Earth Kingdom driven south by the war and bound for Ba Sing Se, proud, orderly and clean to the point of religion, who have feuded with the Zhang for a hundred years over a sacred orb and a thief. They camp at the rim of the Great Divide and will not cross with the Zhang. A stranger is offered washed water and a lecture on hygiene; a dirty stranger is offered the lecture. One sworn to the Gan Jin keeps the tribe's rules, which are many, and rises by keeping them where the Zhang can see.

lore.name: Gan Jin-Zhang conflict
lore.info: The Gan Jin and the Zhang are two Earth Kingdom tribes who have hated each other for as long as either remembers, and each tells the feud's beginning its own way. Both stories start a hundred years ago with a sacred crystal orb that had to be carried from the great eastern gate to the great western gate for an old ritual. The Gan Jin say their patriarch Jin Wei was carrying it when a Zhang named Wei Jin knocked him down and stole it. The Zhang say Wei Jin found Jin Wei hurt on the road and offered to tend him, was told to carry the orb on instead, and was thrown in prison for twenty years by the Gan Jin when he reached the western gate. Neither tribe will share a camp, a meal or a road with the other, and a guide who takes both on one journey earns his fee.

lore.name: Gemsbok bull
lore.info: The gemsbok bull is a heavy, muscular bovine with a bull's frame and the colours of a desert antelope: light brown above, cream below and on the legs, with dark brown borders at the knees and belly and dark stripes running from the eyes down the face. Its long black horns are nearly straight. In Ba Sing Se most people know them only from the city zoo, where a small group stands in a pen far too small for them, looking as miserable as cattle can. The zoo sees few visitors, and its keeper is glad of anyone who comes to look at the sad cages.

lore.name: Geography of the World of Avatar
lore.info: The world is four nations laid over a map of land and sea. The Earth Kingdom holds the Great Continent in the east, the largest and most crowded country there is, with the Si Wong Desert at its heart and the Foggy Swamp in its south-west.
