The Fire Nation lies in the west along the equator, an archipelago of volcanic islands. The two Water Tribes keep the poles, one at each end of the world, north and south of the Earth Kingdom. The Air Nomads had no country at all, only four temples set at the four quarters of the compass: north, south, east and west. Each people shaped its land to its element and was shaped by it in turn, so a traveller can tell where he is from the roofs, the food and the way a stranger is greeted. Between the nations lie open seas, and on those seas, for a hundred years, the Fire Navy has decided who travels and who does not.

lore.name: Giant fly
lore.info: In the bogs of the Earth Kingdom, and above all in the Foggy Swamp, lives a fly the size of a man's forearm, with big compound eyes, long antennae and wings too small for its body, so it flies clumsily and is easy to catch. The Foggy Swamp Tribe hunts giant flies for food and serves them roasted whole to guests at the evening meal. Outsiders who have eaten one say it is better than it looks. Travellers lost in the swamp for days and seeing strange things in the fog are told by the swamp folk to eat something before they decide what they saw.

lore.name: Goat dog
lore.info: The goat dog is a small, squat animal with a long, shaggy white coat that hangs to the ground, curtained over its face and parting at a brown nose. It has stout legs ending in hoof-like feet, erect little ears and a fluffy tail. Goat dogs eat mostly grass, keep calm around people and are kept as pets in Ba Sing Se and across the Earth Kingdom. Farmers use them as lawnmowers that walk: a few goat dogs turned onto a yard keep the grass even. They herd themselves, so they need no shepherd. A goat dog will come to almost anyone who offers it a handful of greens, which is why they so often turn up in other people's yards.

lore.name: Goat gorilla
lore.info: Goat gorillas live in the mountains and forests of the Earth Kingdom, well away from towns. They are built like great apes, with goat's horns, two tusks jutting up from the lower jaw, hanging ears and a hide of dark red or murky white. In the wild they are fiercely territorial: an intruder is charged and rammed, and the heavy arms come down like hammers. An adult can tear a person apart. They eat plants and small animals, lop-eared rabbits especially, and carry their pups on their backs. Raised from a pup they become docile and strong workers; the king of Omashu keeps one as a pet. Hunters' advice: give their country a wide berth, and never step between an adult and a pup.

lore.name: Gondola
lore.info: The prison on the Boiling Rock stands on a volcanic island in the middle of a lake of boiling water, and the only safe way across is a pair of gondolas on pulley cables. Two enclosed cars with open windows run on parallel lines in opposite directions; when one is at the prison station, the other waits at the station on the crater rim, and they pass in the middle. New prisoners come in on them and the guards ride them between shifts. Guards say no one escapes the Boiling Rock, and the cable is most of the reason. Whoever controls the stations controls the island.

lore.name: Grand Secretariat of Ba Sing Se
lore.info: The Grand Secretariat heads the government of Ba Sing Se and, through it, of the Earth Kingdom. The office answers to the Earth King and is his foremost adviser on the city's affairs, and it keeps law and order in the capital through the Dai Li. In practice it oversees every resource of the city, the army included, and decides what reaches the king and what does not. Long Feng holds it now. A petition to the throne goes through the secretariat's clerks, and a request to meet the king takes six to eight weeks at the least to be processed, if it is ever processed at all. A stranger who wants anything done in Ba Sing Se deals with the secretariat; a stranger who wants the secretariat to forget him should never have written to it.

lore.name: Hair loopies
lore.info: Hair loopies are the hairstyle of Water Tribe women: two locks drawn back from the temples and fastened behind, so that they hang in loops either side of the face. In the South they are worn plain and loose; in the North they are often braided into elaborate designs, and a girl of high birth may let two great loops fall from a high tail. Women of both tribes wear them from girlhood to old age, grandmothers as much as granddaughters, and a girl who has worn them since she was small counts them part of who she is. Anywhere away from the poles the style marks a woman as Water Tribe at a glance, so a Water Tribe woman travelling unseen in the Fire Nation lets them down before anything else.

lore.name: Hama's inn
lore.info: The inn in the small mountain town on one of the central Fire Islands is a two-storey house with steps up from the street to a high ground floor. Downstairs are a front room lined with cupboards of food and goods, a dining room and a kitchen where the innkeeper cooks for her guests; upstairs, four bedrooms around a hall, three of them let to travellers, and a steep stair to a locked attic. Behind the house is a large barn full of hay. Though every room has a window, the place has a gloomy, neglected air even by day. Its former owner disappeared some years ago, nobody says how, and the old woman who took it over is known in town for her kindness and her hot spiced tea. Guests are told to be indoors before the full moon rises.

lore.name: Headpieces
lore.info: Across the nations, a top-knot is finished with a headpiece, and the headpiece says who wears it. Fire Nation commoners tie theirs with cloth or bands with small flame shapes. Princes and princesses wear a three-pronged flame in gold. The crown prince's ancient two-pronged crown was given by Sozin to the young Avatar Roku and has not been seen since Roku died. The Fire Lord alone wears the five-pronged golden flame, passed down for generations. In the Earth Kingdom the king wears a domed, conical crown with a small spike, generals wear large headpieces of rank, and Ba Sing Se's women officials wear wide green hair claws. A stranger can read rank from a top-knot before a word is said.

lore.name: Healing
lore.info: Healing is the gentle side of waterbending. The healer wraps water around a wound, the water glows, and the bender steers the body's own energy into the hurt so that it closes far faster than it would alone. It works best on burns, cuts and bruises; it does much less against fever or wasting sickness, and the healer's skill and the purity of the water decide how much can be done. For grave injuries a patient may be laid in water up to the neck. Very rarely a waterbender heals by instinct, untaught. In the Northern Water Tribe healing is the art taught to women and only to women, and its great healers are honoured elders. In a war that burns so many, a waterbender who heals is worth more to a village than any fighter.

lore.name: Hermit crab
lore.info: The mittened hermit crab is a small, white-furred crab with beady black eyes, curly antennae and brown pincers, living in damp, dark corners of the Northern Air Temple. Like any hermit crab it lives in a borrowed shell and trades it for a new one when it outgrows or cracks the old. Together with the fireflies, these crabs are almost the only creatures left from the days when monks lived on the mountain, and the settlers who moved into the empty temple are fond of them for it: born there or not, the crabs made the old place their home. They are harmless and easy to pick up.

lore.name: High Sage
lore.info: The High Sage leads the Fire Sages, chosen by the other sages through a process of their own, and lives at the High Temple in the Fire Nation Capital, ready to serve the government when it calls. In ancient times the Fire Lords themselves led the sages, until one Fire Lord set himself apart as a secular ruler and left the temples to the sages; since then High Sages have led them. A High Sage crowned Fire Lord Ozai in 95 AG, and the office crowns each new Fire Lord. The sages once served the Avatar; since Sozin's day they have served the Fire Lord alone, and the High Sage's counsel goes where the throne wants it. The office's headgear is crowned with a golden flame. A stranger at the High Temple speaks to the lesser sages first, and to the High Sage only if spoken to.

lore.name: History of the World of Avatar
lore.info: Ask an Earth Kingdom elder how the world came to be as it is, and the answer begins with the four nations: the Water Tribes at the poles, the Earth Kingdom across the great continent, the Fire Nation on its islands and the Air Nomads in their mountain temples. Each people learned its bending from the first masters of its element. The Water Tribes watched the moon pull the tides, earthbenders learned from the badgermoles, the Air Nomads from the flying bison and firebenders from the dragons. Above the four stands the Avatar, reborn in each nation in turn to keep the balance between them and with the spirits. Most of what common folk know of the past is told in the lives of the Avatar and in war: Kyoshi and the conqueror, Roku and the colonies, then the comet, and a century of fighting since.

lore.name: How Kyoshi Island became an island
lore.info: Kyoshi Island was not always an island. It was once a peninsula on the southern coast of the Earth Kingdom, a poor place of farmers and fishermen that merchant ships passed by. When Chin the Conqueror had taken almost the entire Earth Kingdom and marched his armies to its neck, the Avatar Kyoshi, who had made her home there, split the peninsula from the mainland and set it adrift as an island, so that no army could reach it on foot. Chin did not survive the day. The islanders have honoured her ever since: every village keeps a statue of Kyoshi, one has made a temple into her shrine, and the warriors who guard the island fight with fans and paint their faces in her style. Its villages trade elephant koi to restaurants all over the kingdom, but some of them have never let a stranger stay the night.

lore.name: How the dragons were hunted out
lore.info: Dragons are the great horned, whiskered serpents of the Fire Nation, some with wings and some without, and the old belief is that firebending was learned from them. For a long time they were honoured: they are carved over temple doors, and Roku, the Fire Nation's own Avatar, rode one. Fire Lord Sozin began hunting them. Whoever killed a dragon took the honorary name of Dragon, and nobles hunted them for the glory of that name. Hunted dragons turned savage and the hunts grew, until within living memory they stopped being seen at all. Iroh, the Fire Lord's elder brother, is called the Dragon of the West, and the Fire Nation says he killed the last one. Any dragon scale, bone or tooth found today comes from the hunting years.

lore.name: How the Great Divide was made
lore.info: The Great Divide is the largest canyon in the world, cut through the rocky middle of the Earth Kingdom, and nobody agrees on how it came to be. Many people of the region believe that the earth spirits tore it open in rage when the farmers who lived here stopped bringing them their offerings; others say it is the slow work of wind and water over ages beyond counting. Either way, the canyon is not a friendly place. The only way down is a narrow path along the cliff wall, sections of which crumble without warning, and the floor belongs to the canyon crawlers, which can smell food from a great distance. A canyon guide, an earthbender who knows the trail and can mend it, takes parties across in a day, and the first rule at his station is that every scrap of food is left behind.

lore.name: Hundred Year War
lore.info: The war began in 0 AG, when Fire Lord Sozin used the comet's power to destroy the Air Nomads and strike the Earth Kingdom and the Water Tribes in the same season. He called it sharing the Fire Nation's peace and wealth with the world. The world calls it the Hundred Year War, and by the winter of 99 AG it is very nearly won. The Air Nomads are gone. The Southern Water Tribe has been raided until hardly a waterbender remains. The Fire Nation holds most of the Earth Kingdom's west and north, plants colonies on the continent, and patrols every sea with iron ships that burn coal. Three powers still stand against it: the Northern Water Tribe behind its ice, King Bumi's Omashu, and Ba Sing Se behind its walls. Steam engines, tanks and trebuchets fight provincial lords, ostrich horse cavalry and earthbenders. Nobody alive remembers peace, and the Avatar who should have ended the war has not been seen in a hundred years.

lore.name: Hybrid pigs
lore.info: The farms of the Earth Kingdom and the Fire Nation run on half-pigs. The moo-sow, half cow, gives the rich pig-milk country people love and good meat; wild ones roam the forests of the Fire Islands, and the army uses tame ones in training. The picken, a pig-headed chicken, lays eggs and is the poor village's bird, though it catches sickness easily. The pigster, a pink-feathered pig-rooster, wakes the farm at dawn. The wooly-pig is shorn for wool, always muddy because it loves to roll in muck. There are also antlered deer-pigs, rabbit pigs and the bull pig, known for eating bones. A bull pig is also something a farmer says when he hears a lie.

lore.name: Ice Dodging
lore.info: Ice dodging is the Southern Water Tribe's rite of passage, taken at fourteen. The young sailor steers a small cutter through a field of shifting ice in rough water, with friends at the mainsail and the jib, and the whole crew comes through together or not at all. Afterwards the father, or an elder warrior in his place, marks each one on the forehead for what they showed: the brave, who held the mainsail against the wind; the trusted, who kept the jib steady; the wise, who steered and led. The marks are painted for that day, but the honour is remembered for life. Since the warriors left in 97 AG there has been no father to take the boys out, and a son who turned fourteen after that has waited for his rite ever since.

lore.name: Iceberg spike
lore.info: The seas around Agna Qel'a are sown with iceberg spikes: jagged false bergs raised by waterbenders, strong enough to rip through a steel hull. Set where the currents run hard, they sink even large ships, and benders can raise new ones from a boat in moments. They are also hiding places: warriors of the north wait behind them in canoes to fall on a ship that slows among the ice. The southern waterbenders used the same art to trap Fire Nation ships during the early raids. Northern masters teach a smaller form of it to their students as a way to pin an opponent in a sparring match.

lore.name: Iguana seal
lore.info: Iguana seals bask and swim around the outlying islands of the Fire Nation, where the water is warm: an iguana's body and spiny crest on a seal's flippers, green or blue, with a dark ridge of thorny spikes from skull to tail. Their call carries far over water and sounds eerily like singing. For generations sailors believed it was mermaids, steered toward the rocks to find them, and found only seals. Disappointed crews ate them, and sailors still do. Old sailors still tell young ones that the singing on the rocks is a mermaid, and the young ones still believe it for a night.

lore.name: Infamy in the Four Nations
lore.info: Every nation has its own law, and every nation agrees on this: a killing that served nothing is remembered. Word travels faster than any traveller, along the roads, the ferries and the messenger hawks. The Fire Nation posts wanted notices; the Dai Li keep files; the Water Tribes simply remember faces. A name that becomes notorious closes the respectable doors first, then the ferries and the coaches, and at the last brings guards who do not ask questions and hunters who are paid not to. Bloodbending a person is a crime in every nation that knows it exists. The only way back that anyone remembers is the old one: penance at the Avatar Sanctuary of the Southern Air Temple, slowly, among the statues of every Avatar who came before.

lore.name: Jackalope
lore.info: The jackalope is a long-eared desert hare with a cleft lip, a tufted tail, strong leaping legs and a small pair of antlers. It lives in the Si Wong Desert and eats cactus, thorns and all. It is unaffected by the juice that sends people out of their minds, and it nibbles quietly so as not to draw predators. Jackalopes are timid: a startled one springs straight up into the air and is gone. A thirsty traveller who sees one at a cactus should not reason that what is safe for the jackalope is safe for him.

lore.name: Jin Wei
lore.info: Jin Wei is the patriarch of the Gan Jin, an earthbender warrior who, a hundred years ago, was chosen to carry the tribe's sacred crystal orb from the great eastern gate to the great western gate in its redemption ritual. Gan Jin children learn that as he neared the western post, a Zhang man named Wei Jin knocked him down and stole the orb, and that this theft began the feud. To the Zhang, Jin Wei is a weakling who dropped his duty and never thanked the man who finished it. Say his name kindly near the Great Divide and half the canyon will hear you take a side.

lore.name: Keeping a sky bison
lore.info: Flying bison lived beside the Air Nomads at every air temple, and the monks held that the bison were the first airbenders. A young nomad chose a calf, and the two stayed together for life; it took years to train one properly. A grown bison weighs tons and has six legs and a broad, flat tail it steers with. It grazes treetops, eats hay, fruit and vegetables gladly, and has toes clever enough to hold a person gently. Keepers cleared the mud from between those toes when grooming. The word to fly is yip yip, and a bison whistle calls one from far away with a note no person can hear. The northern monks played polo in the air on bisonback. Calves cannot fly for their first weeks, and their parents attack anyone they do not trust who comes near them. Since the temples fell, nobody has seen a living bison, and a bison whistle is a keepsake with nothing to call.

lore.name: Knowledge Seekers
lore.info: The spirit Wan Shi Tong keeps fox-like servants who range the whole world gathering what people write down: scrolls, codices, maps, old letters. They are brown with pale patches, quick and silent, and they cross between the Spirit World and this one as easily as a dog crosses a yard. In the Si Wong Desert a traveller may see one trotting over a dune with a scroll in its jaws, heading for the tower that is the top of the buried library. Inside, they fetch books for patrons who cannot find them, and they expect a treat for the trouble. They are tireless, and the library grows every year they live. A stranger should not chase one or try to take what it carries; what a seeker brings home belongs to its master now.

lore.name: Komodo rhinos in the Fire Army
lore.info: The komodo rhino is the Fire Nation's war beast, bred for war, for hauling and for meat. It has a lizard's jaws and tail on a rhinoceros body, small mammal ears, short clawed feet and three great horns: two sweeping down from the brow, one up from the snout. Its hide is said to be tough as steel, and spears and swords break on it, which only makes it angrier. Charging, it can punch through a wall. The army decks them in red, every recruit learns to mount and ride one in training, and Fire Nation sausage is made from komodo meat. Wild ones are calmer than army-bred ones, unless their young are threatened. Do not stand in front of one.

lore.name: Kyoshi Warriors
lore.info: An order of female warriors named for Avatar Kyoshi, who founded them to keep her island, one band to each village, fighting with war fans, face paint and footwork no army teaches and keeping Kyoshi Island apart from the war. In the winter of 99 AG a band under Suki leaves to help the defenceless on the mainland. A stranger on the island is tied to a post by them until proven harmless; a Fire Nation stranger stays tied. One sworn to the warriors learns the fans, the paint and the stance, and rises by the band's trust and a captain's nod.

lore.name: Lavabending
lore.info: Every child on Kyoshi Island knows how the island came to be. When a conqueror marched on the peninsula where Avatar Kyoshi lived, she split the land from the mainland, tearing fissures and pulling molten rock up from beneath until the sea poured in. Earthbenders call it lavabending: turning stone to liquid fire and back, and steering it where they wish. Fire Nation islanders have their own stories of Avatars who woke volcanoes or turned a lava flow aside. No ordinary earthbender is known to have done it. It is a legend of the Avatars, and an earthbender who boasts of it near a volcano will get no audience but the sulphur.

lore.name: Law in Ba Sing Se
lore.info: Ba Sing Se has more law than anywhere in the world, and most of it is never written down. The Dai Li keep the city for the Grand Secretariat, Long Feng, in the name of an Earth King nobody sees. The first rule is the one no one says aloud: the war is never spoken of inside these walls, and whoever mentions it, above all in the Upper Ring, is visited by quiet men in green robes and stone gloves. Each ring keeps its own people, and a resident of the Lower Ring needs leave to pass the gate inward. Newcomers are given a cultural ambassador who smiles, shows them the sights and reports where they went. Those who keep talking stop being seen in their street, and their neighbours learn not to ask. Bounty hunters get nothing here; the Dai Li need no help. A stranger must not speak of the war, must not ask to see the Earth King, must not cross a ring wall without papers, and must not refuse the tour.

lore.name: Law in Capital Island
lore.info: On Capital Island the law is the Fire Lord's word, and the Domestic Forces keep it: they patrol the harbour steps, hold the Great Gates of Azulon and guard the Capital City Prison. Sedition is the gravest crime, and sedition is wide: speaking against Fire Lord Ozai, aiding the Avatar or any enemy of the nation, deserting the colours, questioning the war in front of a teacher. Failing to bow before a member of the royal family is an insult answered by prostration or by an Agni Kai. Wanted notices go up in the plaza with a face and a reward, and the hunters who answer them are paid by the crown. A stranger must carry papers and a reason, keep his voice down near the palace, never wear Water Tribe blue in the streets, and never touch a noble's hair. Infamy here is quick: one rumour at the docks, and the guards at the gates already know the name.

lore.name: Law in Kolau and the South-West
lore.info: In Kolau the law is Omashu's, and Omashu's law is its king's. Earthbender guards hold the gate and the delivery chutes, a thief or a spy is brought before the throne, and the King of Omashu is known to judge in ways no one can predict. Outside the walls the law thins fast. In the plains villages Earth Kingdom soldiers billet where they like and take what they want, and a farmer who complains gets no hearing; some villages pay the soldiers, some the bandits, some both. The Foggy Swamp Tribe keep their own ways and want no outsiders among their trees. A stranger must not ride the delivery chutes for sport, must not firebend within sight of Omashu, must not cut wood in the swamp, and must not refuse a soldier openly in a village where the soldiers rule. The wanted are hunted here by whoever is paid, and in the plains that is often the soldiers themselves.

lore.name: Law in Si Wong and the Plains
lore.info: Nobody rules the Si Wong Desert, so nothing there is a crime and everything is a feud. The Si Wong tribes hold the sand by clan; a wrong done to one sandbender is a wrong done to his whole tribe, and they answer it themselves. The Misty Palms Oasis has a cantina and no constable, and the beetle-headed merchants buy whatever is brought to them without asking where it came from. On the plains the Gan Jin and the Zhang have kept a feud for a hundred years over a wrong neither tells the same way, and a traveller who walks with one is the other's enemy. The Rough Rhinos camp on the desert's edge and take contracts on anyone with a price. A stranger must not take a sand-sailer that is not his, must not drink a tribe's water without leave, and must not cross the sand without a guide. A killing here is never posted; the dead man's kin simply remember it.

lore.name: Law in the Fire Islands
lore.info: Across the Fire Islands each town has its mayor or governor, appointed from the capital; the Domestic Forces keep the streets and Fire Navy patrols keep the harbours, while on Crescent Island the Fire Sages keep their own temple rules. The crimes are the capital's crimes, sedition first and desertion close behind: a deserter's face is posted in every port, and the navy pays well for it. Fire Fountain City and Jang Hui answer to their officials, Ember Island to whichever noble family owns the beach. The worst prisoners go to the Boiling Rock, a prison in a boiling lake that no one has ever escaped. A stranger must not ask what the war costs, must not bend water or earth where anyone can see, and must not sleep on a rich family's sand. The islands are close and gossip rides the ferries: a needless killing on one island is talk on the next by morning.

lore.name: Law in the Lakes and the Serpent's Pass
lore.info: The Lakes belong to Ba Sing Se's bureaucracy, and the bureaucracy's law is paper. At Full Moon Bay the ferry station takes refugees across to the city, and nobody boards without a passport stamped by the passport attendant; a forged passport is the commonest crime at the station and the easiest to be caught with. Clerks take bribes, tickets go to those who pay, and a family without papers is sent to the Serpent's Pass on foot. On the pass itself there is no law but the serpent in the strait below. Earth Kingdom soldiers guard the ferries against fire, and a firebender found aboard is a prisoner on the spot. Bounty hunters are not welcome at the station; they wait on the far side of the pass. A stranger must not carry fire onto a ferry, must not travel on a passport that is not his, and must not take the Serpent's Pass alone.

lore.name: Law in the Mo Ce Coast
lore.info: The Mo Ce Coast has two laws, and they are at war. Where the Fire Nation colonies hold, a colonial mayor rules beside a garrison commander, and earthbending in an occupied village is a crime that ends on the prison rig offshore. Where the Earth Kingdom still holds, General Fong's officers keep a soldier's law and look hard at any able stranger who will not enlist. In the forests between, the Freedom Fighters keep their own rules in the trees, and the Fire Nation calls them bandits; at the Pohuai Stronghold the Yuyan Archers hold the colonies' northern edge. Pirates and smugglers trade openly at the seedy merchants pier, which asks no names. A stranger must not earthbend in sight of a garrison, must not ask a colonist which side he is on, and must not take the Freedom Fighters' help without asking what it will cost. Bounty hunters work this coast more than any other.

lore.name: Law in the Northern Mountains
lore.info: The Taihua Mountains have no ruler, and the cold is the only law everyone obeys. In the Northern Air Temple a colony of refugees lives under the mechanist who rebuilt it, and his word is the colony's law: share the work, keep out of his workshops, and treat the old temple as his. Down the slopes the Fire Nation keeps garrisons in the passes and takes any armed stranger for a deserter or a rebel. At Chameleon Bay the warriors of the Southern Water Tribe hold their inlet under their own chief, and a stranger who comes by water is an enemy until he proves otherwise. Han Tui remembers a battle and little else. A stranger must not take shelter in the temple without the mechanist's leave, must not light a fire where the passes can see it, and must not come up on Chameleon Bay in a red boat. Wanted men come here to vanish, and the mountains usually let them.

lore.name: Law in the Northern Water Tribe
lore.info: In Agna Qel'a the chief is the law: Chief Arnook judges crimes, hears disputes and commands the warriors. The custom of the North, as it stands in the winter of 99 AG, is old and strict. A woman of the tribe may learn waterbending only to heal; fighting with water is for men, and Master Pakku, who teaches the warriors, will not take a girl as his student. At sixteen a girl's marriage is arranged and her betrothal necklace carved. The Spirit Oasis is sacred, and no one goes into it to make trouble. The North has no bounty hunters and no need of them: a stranger who reaches the sea gate is watched until he leaves. A stranger must not bring a ship of the Fire Nation into the iceberg fields, must not enter the oasis without leave, must not court a betrothed girl, and must not ask a woman of the tribe to fight him.

lore.name: Law in the South
lore.info: The South has no lord, no court and no jail. With the warriors gone with Hakoda since 97 AG, the villages keep order the old way: the elders decide, Kanna first among them at Wolf Cove, and the heaviest punishment is to be turned away from the tribe and its stores. Everyone is kin to some degree, so a theft from the stores is a theft from every family. The raids taught one law above the rest: a waterbender is hidden, never named to a stranger. No bounty hunter comes this far; what comes instead are Fire Navy ships, and the village treats any stranger as their scout until he proves otherwise. A stranger must not come ashore armed, must not ask who in the village bends, and must not take from the ice stores without being given.

lore.name: Law in the Southern Coast
lore.info: The war has not reached the south coast, and its law shows it: every town keeps its own. In Gaoling the magistrates answer to the great families, the Beifong family first, and an insult to a rich house is a crime there when a robbery in the poor quarter is not. Earth Rumble fights are not quite lawful and nobody stops them. Chin Village keeps a jail and long memories, and a stranger who tries to pay in Water Tribe money is turned away. On Kyoshi Island the villages keep their own counsel under their headmen, the Kyoshi Warriors are their guard, and an uninvited stranger is tied up first and questioned after. Bounty hunters rest in Gaoling's inns between contracts. A stranger must not land on Kyoshi Island without being asked, must not speak ill of Kyoshi there, and must not believe the war cannot come this far.

lore.name: Law in the Spirit World
lore.info: There is no human law in the Spirit World and no human justice. The spirits keep their own rules, older and stranger than any king's. Koh, the face stealer, takes the face of anyone who shows him an expression, so a traveller in his realm keeps his face still and his fear behind it. Wan Shi Tong keeps a library of all knowledge and wants in it only those who come to learn, never those who would use it for war. A spirit whose forest has been burned, as Hei Bai's was, does not ask which human did it. There is no infamy here and no price on any head, but a spirit remembers an insult far longer than a man does. A visitor must not lie to a spirit about why he came, must not take what is not freely offered, and should not try to bend: without the body, no element answers.

lore.name: Life in the Earth Kingdom
lore.info: The Earth Kingdom is too big to have one way of life. Most of its people live in farming villages, hamlets of a few families and the odd market town, a great many more crowd into Ba Sing Se and Omashu, and the rest live on the roads as nomads, traders and refugees. It has no single law: each state, town and village keeps its own code, the farther from Ba Sing Se the freer, and corruption is simply how things are done. What every Earth Kingdom family shares is a care for face, its good name in the eyes of others, and respect for its elders and ancestors. Rice is the staple and tea the common drink, and accents change from valley to valley. Spring is the earth's season, when earthbenders are strongest. A stranger who shames a family in public has made an enemy for a generation.

lore.name: Life in the Water Tribes
lore.info: The Water Tribes are a people of the ice and the sea: the Northern Water Tribe in its city at the North Pole, the Southern Water Tribe in its villages at the South, and far away the Foggy Swamp Tribe in the Earth Kingdom's swamp, kin by descent and very different in their ways. Family is everything; every member of a tribe counts the others as kin to some degree, and children are named for relatives. Generosity is a point of honour, and the open hand of a Water Tribe trader is a byword in other lands. They live by hunting and fishing, keep stores on the ice through the long dark, dress in fur and hide, and eat sea prunes, seal jerky and whatever the sea gives up. Winter is their season, when waterbenders are strongest. A guest is fed before he is asked his business.

lore.name: Lightning generation
lore.info: A handful of firebenders can make lightning. They split the energy within the body into its two halves, let the halves crash back together, and send the bolt out through the fingertips. Firebenders call it the cold-blooded fire, because it wants a calm mind and a still heart rather than rage, and it kills where ordinary fire only burns. For most of history the art was thought a myth or a lost thing. The Fire Nation found it again, and keeps it for the royal family's inner circle and its highest officers. A common soldier will never be taught it. Anyone who sees a crackle of blue-white light in a firebender's hand should not wait to see where it goes.

lore.name: Lightning redirection
lore.info: Old soldiers in Fire Nation garrisons tell a story they cannot prove: that there is a way to take a bolt of lightning into the body without dying of it, draw it down and out again, and throw it somewhere else. Nobody can say who first claimed it, and nobody has met anyone who saw it done. Others say no such art exists and the tale was made up to comfort recruits who had seen what a bolt does to a man. It is a campfire story, told the way soldiers everywhere tell stories about a weapon that can be beaten.

lore.name: Lion turtle
lore.info: Sailors on the far seas tell of an island that is not an island: a turtle so vast that forest grows on its shell, with the maned head of a lion under the waterline. The tales call it the oldest creature in the world, older than the four nations, and say that before people bent the elements they bent the energy within themselves, and that the lion turtles knew that art. No person living has learned it. Scholars in Ba Sing Se file all of this under legend, and no chart marks where one might be found. If a fisherman swears the island he anchored by was gone in the morning, the polite answer is to buy him another cup.

lore.name: Lop-eared rabbit
lore.info: The lop-eared rabbit is a little white rabbit with grey patches round its eyes and ears longer than its whole body. It is common wild in the Earth Kingdom and a popular pet. Those ears give it hearing sharp enough that catching one in the open is close to impossible: it is easily frightened, very fast and gone down a hole before a hunter is in reach. Goat gorillas hunt them, so a field full of skittish rabbits can mean one is near. A rabbit raised by hand loses its fear and makes a gentle companion, and many Earth Kingdom children keep one.

lore.name: Lu Ten
lore.info: Lu Ten was Iroh's only son and, after his father, the next in line to the Fire Nation throne. He served in the Fire Army and went with his father to the walls of Ba Sing Se, where he was killed in the fighting around the time the Outer Wall was breached. His death ended the siege as surely as any defender did: Iroh withdrew soon after and has not commanded an army since. With no grandson of his eldest line left, the succession turned. When Fire Lord Azulon died, the court announced that his dying wish named the younger son, Ozai, and Iroh did not contest it. Lu Ten's birthday fell in spring, and his father is said to grieve him still.

lore.name: Manatee whale
lore.info: In the warm seas around the Fire Islands the manatee whale floats about eating seaweed, a huge maroon-backed beast with a tan belly, small eyes, a fat whiskered snout and the body of a whale. Islanders call them the whale cows of the sea. Tamed ones are harnessed to pull boats that have neither engine nor sail; a single animal tows a loaded launch to Ember Island and back without noticing the weight. They swim faster than they look when pressed, though nothing like an elephant koi, and they care very little about what goes on around them, which is why even children can ride one. A noble family's pleasure boat drawn by a manatee whale is a common sight in the holiday months.

lore.name: Marriage in the Four Nations
lore.info: Each nation marries in its own way. In the Northern Water Tribe a girl's marriage is arranged when she turns sixteen, and her betrothed carves a stone pendant and fastens it to a choker; once she wears it she is spoken for, and every other young man knows it. Such necklaces are handed down, and a grandmother's may travel far from the tribe it was carved in. In the South people choose their own spouses. In the Fire Nation most people marry for love, nobles included, and only the royal family is known to marry for policy; a wedding there is a feast, with red and white gowns, lanterns of flowers and a sage or a village elder presiding, though a Fire Lord may preside if he pleases. A stranger courting across these customs should learn first which one he is standing in.

lore.name: Meadow vole
lore.info: Meadow voles are tiny white rodents with a bare stub of a tail, common in the forests of the Earth Kingdom. They live on seeds and fruit, squeak a great deal and are unusually friendly; one will climb onto a still hand that offers it something to eat. Foresters say they are worth watching. A vole senses people coming long before a human ear catches anything, and one that suddenly squeaks and bolts from a clearing is often warning of riders or soldiers on the path. Winged lemurs and other small hunters catch them easily.

lore.name: Metalbending
lore.info: Every earthbender learns early that metal cannot be bent. Iron and steel are made from earth, but the smiths have purified them, and what is left gives a bender nothing to hold. The masters say it plainly and the students repeat it: earth moves, metal does not. The Fire Nation has built its whole war on that rule, with iron tanks, metal-plated ships, steel cells and walls of plate, and it holds its earthbender prisoners on metal rigs at sea for the same reason. An earthbender who claims to have bent a sword or dented a hull is either a liar or a fool, and in any Earth Kingdom tavern they will be laughed out of the room. No one in history has ever done it.

lore.name: Military of the Earth Kingdom
lore.info: The armed forces of the Earth Kingdom, an army, a navy and the specialised divisions that have held the Fire Nation off for most of a hundred years: earthbender regiments in green, the garrisons of the free cities, General Fong's fortress on the west coast, the Outer Wall's defenders and the Council of Five over all of it. It has lost the west and the colonies and held the walls. A stranger is a recruit or a refugee to be sent on; a Fire Nation stranger is a prisoner. One sworn to the military marches in green, holds a wall or a fort, and rises by the council's notice, which comes slowly and to the living.

lore.name: Military of the Fire Nation
lore.info: The Fire Nation's armed forces are the strongest in the world: the Fire Army, second in numbers only to the Earth Kingdom's; the Fire Navy, the largest of all; and the Domestic Forces at home. The Fire Lord commands them and delegates through a few high generals and admirals, while the war minister oversees new weapons and machines. The army holds firebenders and nonbenders alike, with infantry, cavalry, artillery and tanks. Women have become rare at the front and mostly serve in the Domestic Forces, which police the homeland, guard its prisons and train recruits for every branch. Special units serve beside the line: the Yuyan Archers, the Rough Rhinos, the Southern Raiders, and the imperial firebenders who guard the royal family. A widely known proverb holds that all warfare is based on deception. Propaganda fills the ranks, and promotion goes to the bold.

lore.name: Military of the Water Tribe
lore.info: The Water Tribes have no army to match the other nations; each tribe defends itself. The North keeps warriors under its chief, waterbenders and nonbenders both, armed with clubs, bone spears, scimitars and machetes edged with whale teeth, and its master waterbenders hold the ramparts of Agna Qel'a. No woman serves among them. A field of iceberg spikes off the city has torn open Fire Navy hulls for most of the war, and the North's catamarans thread it easily. The South was always defended by a village militia; after the raids took its benders, its warriors were nonbenders with clubs, boomerangs and spears, and in 97 AG they sailed away under Hakoda in wolf-headed armour to fight the Fire Navy. They fight by sabotage and ambush, and they make the most of very little.

lore.name: Mo Ce Sea
lore.info: The Mo Ce Sea is the open water between the western Earth Kingdom and the eastern Fire Islands, warm in the south and mild in the north, crossed by traders since long before the war. Its islands are few and small. Crescent Island and its fire temple stand in it, and so does the seedy merchants pier, where a ship can buy anything that has been stolen. For a century the sea has been a battlefield, and the Fire Navy holds a blockade along the edge of its home waters to keep every outsider out; ships that cross the line without papers are sunk or taken, and fireballs are thrown at anything that flies. The Fire Nation also anchors a prison rig out here where captured earthbenders, far from any earth, build its ships. The water is rich with fish. Fishermen of both nations work it carefully, and none of them go near the blockade.

lore.name: Monorail
lore.info: The monorail carries Ba Sing Se's people from ring to ring. Earthbent stone arches carry the rail over the great roads between the walls, and each car is pushed along by two earthbenders standing at its back. Inside are benches, hand bars for those who must stand, and paper windows that keep out the wind. The trains keep a fixed timetable and run late into the night, but a ride needs a ticket and the passport to go with it, and most of the Lower Ring cannot afford the fare. Ticket clerks are strict with newcomers; papers that look forged will not get past them.

lore.name: Music in the World of Avatar
lore.info: Every nation makes music, and most of it is song: folk songs easy to learn on the road and old enough that nobody remembers who made them. The tsungi horn, a curved and polished metal horn, is thought to come from the Fire Nation, where it is most played, and Fire Nation schools teach music as a formal class where students march in place rather than dance. The alley shops of Ba Sing Se sell moon-round lutes, four-stringed liuqin, zithers with movable bridges and bronze bells. Gongs hang in the palaces of the Earth King and the Fire Lord alike. The Air Nomads blew long horns that sounded a single low note and echoed through the mountains. Wandering singers walk the Earth Kingdom roads with an instrument under the robe and a love song for every village, and a traveller who can sing rarely goes hungry.

lore.name: Names in the Four Nations
lore.info: A name often tells a stranger where its owner was born. Water Tribe names tend to carry a hard k and an open ah, and children are named for relatives, so the same names come round in every family. Fire Nation names lean on a sharp z, royal names most of all, and yet the commonest Fire Nation name, Lee, is so common that half the boys in any Fire Nation town answer to it; a stranger who needs to hide his own can borrow it safely. Earth Kingdom names follow region and family, and a farmer's son from the plains sounds nothing like a noble of the Upper Ring. A traveller who takes a false name should pick one that fits his face and his accent, because a Water Tribe face with a Fire Nation name draws a second look.

lore.name: North Pole continent
lore.info: The North Pole continent is the world's northernmost land, ringed by the Northern Sea: tundra, polar desert, lake ice and mountains, most of it white the year round. Its southern edge thaws in the warm months, when rivers run, shrubs come up through the snow and the sea ice breaks open. Buffalo yaks, turtle seals and koalaotters live here, and the Northern Water Tribe hunts them. Most of its people live in Agna Qel'a, the city of ice walls and canals at the edge of the sea. The coastal plains are the worst of it. Winter blizzards last for days, and sheet ice that looks solid gives way underfoot, so that even northern hunters and waterbenders cross them quickly or not at all. A southerner who walks out onto the tundra without a guide is not looked for until spring.

lore.name: Northern Sea
lore.info: The Northern Sea is the cold open water between the northern coast of the Great Continent and the North Pole. Agna Qel'a is its great harbour, and the Northern Water Tribe watches it closely: strangers who approach the city by sea or air are met by waterbenders before they see the walls. Fish, squid, giant sea crabs, turtle seals and koalaotters live in it, and its ice packs drift south with the currents in the warm months. In a century of war the Fire Nation has never taken the North, and its captains know that a fleet sailing these waters is sailing toward a city of waterbenders built of the sea itself. Sailors from the south are warned that most of an iceberg lies beneath the water.

lore.name: Northern Water Tribe
lore.info: The chiefdom of the North Pole, the oldest of the Water Tribes, ruled by Chief Arnook from Agna Qel'a and kept for a hundred years by its sea wall, its waterbenders and its isolation. Master Pakku teaches the men to fight and the healers teach the women; its customs are old and hard. It has never fallen and never fought, until the Siege of the North. A stranger is a guest at the chief's feast and a curiosity in the canals; a Fire Nation stranger is a prisoner. One sworn to the tribe keeps the wall, the canals or the hunt, and rises by the chief's word and the master's.

lore.name: Omashu
lore.info: The monarchy and the earthbender army of Omashu, the Earth Kingdom's second city, under King Bumi, who guards its gate, runs its delivery system and supplied the Earth Kingdom's army with troops until the Fire Nation took the city in the spring of 100 AG. Its guards check every cart's cabbages; its king sets challenges for anyone interesting. A stranger is tested, housed and fed, in that order; a Fire Nation stranger is housed first. One sworn to Omashu serves its gate, its chutes or its court, and rises by the king's amusement, which is harder than it looks.

lore.name: Omashu delivery system
lore.info: Omashu sends its mail and goods through a web of stone chutes that winds down the city's mountainside. Earthbenders at the loading points lift each cart to the top of a run, and gravity does the rest: parcels, letters and open carts of fruit rattle down the slides to every quarter. The system is the pride of the city and a trial for its merchants, whose stalls tend to sit where carts come off the rails. The steepest runs are fast enough that bored young nobles have been known to ride them for sport, to the fury of the merchants below. A stranger crossing a street in Omashu should look up as well as both ways.

lore.name: Omashu Resistance
lore.info: The rebels who mean to free Omashu from the Fire Nation after its capture in the spring of 100 AG, earthbenders and ordinary citizens in the sewers and chutes, led by a few of the king's old guards, faking a plague to empty the city and keep its people out of the governor's hands. A stranger is a possible agent until proven otherwise; a Fire Nation stranger is a hostage. One sworn to the resistance moves through the tunnels, carries messages and food, and rises by what they are trusted to know.

lore.name: Organizations in the World of Avatar
lore.info: Much of the world is run by bodies with names. In the Earth Kingdom the Council of Five commands the army from Ba Sing Se, the Dai Li keep the capital, Ba Sing Se University trains its scholars, the Five-Seven-Five Society keeps its poetry strict, and the Royal Earthbender Guards protect the king. The Kyoshi Warriors guard their island and the Terra Team holds the Outer Wall. In the Fire Nation the Fire Sages keep the temples, the Ember Island Players keep the stage, the Fire Nation circus tours the islands, and the military is a world of its own. The Air Nomads had their councils of elders. Other groups have no charter and plenty of members: pirates, the Freedom Fighters of the western forests, the Rough Rhinos. A stranger learns quickly which bodies he must please and which he must avoid.

lore.name: Pai Sho
lore.info: Pai Sho is a game for two, played across the whole world by young and old. The board is round, divided into sections and a grid of coloured squares, and the pieces are round tiles each bearing a picture: the blue lotus, jasmine, the chrysanthemum, the rose, white jade, the rhododendron, knotweed, a boat, a dragon. Legend says the spirits made the game and handed it to mortals to teach them patience and humility. Every culture plays it by its own rules; some play it fast, as a game of chance, others slowly, as a game of strategy, with as many as sixty tiles a side. Monks of the air temples played it, teahouse regulars play it, kings play it. A classic proverb of the board says that a good move for you is a good move for your opponent. A stranger who sits at another man's board should ask the house rules first, and should never take an old man's slow game for a weak one.

lore.name: Painted Lady
lore.info: Along the Jang Hui River the people tell of a river spirit who watches over their town in hard times: a woman with a painted face and a wide hat who protects the town when it is in need and heals its sick. She was once a person, the story goes, so close to the river and its spirits that when she died she stayed with it. Few have seen her; only those with the spiritual eye ever do. Since the Fire Nation Army factory upstream began pouring its sludge into the water, the fish have sickened, the children cough, and the villagers say the Painted Lady has not come for years. Ask about her on the piers and an old fisherman will tell the story, then ask why the spirit would want to come back to water like this.

lore.name: Palanquin
lore.info: Palanquins are how royalty and the high nobility move in public. They are slow, and the slowness is part of the point: the people should see who passes. Fire Nation palanquins are red with gold trim, a cushioned seat behind pink curtains, and a black cloth bearing the national insignia, carried by four bearers. The Earth Kingdom's are larger, built like small temples with a slanted green roof, gold edging and long yellow carrying poles. A royal palanquin may be carried even inside a palace. Stepping into a palanquin's path, or meeting the eyes of the person inside, is a good way to meet its guards.

lore.name: Pao Family Tea House
lore.info: The Pao Family Tea House is a small family tea shop in the Lower Ring of Ba Sing Se, in one of the ring's better streets, where its regulars are guards and delivery workers employed by the richer craftsmen nearby. Two wooden pillars hung with green lanterns frame the door, and the lanterns burn at night to call people in. Inside is one long room: eight square tables with benches, four to a side, paintings of animals on the walls, a counter across the back and, behind it, a small alcove with the stone hearth where the tea is brewed and the cups are washed. The shutters swing wide on warm days. The owner minds every cup and every coin and is always looking for help. Nobody comes for the tea, which is ordinary at best; they come to sit down, talk and be out of the street for an hour.

lore.name: Passports and Papers
lore.info: The war has made papers worth more than coin. Ba Sing Se admits no refugee without a passport, issued and stamped at the ferry station in Full Moon Bay by the passport attendant, and a family without one waits, bribes or walks the Serpent's Pass. Inside the city, papers decide which ring a person may live in and which gates he may pass. On the Fire Nation's home islands an official may ask anyone who is not plainly a citizen for proof of who he is, and a colonist visiting the homeland is wise to carry his family's papers. Forged passports change hands in every refugee camp, and the forgers' best customers are the people who can least afford to be caught with one. A traveller keeps his papers closer than his purse.

lore.name: Piracy in the World of Avatar
lore.info: Piracy has always followed the sea lanes. The Fire Navy keeps the waters of the Fire Islands mostly clear, so pirates work the Earth Kingdom's coasts and rivers and the cold seas toward the South Pole. Most crews sell what they take through smugglers ashore; others sell straight from the deck and turn their ship into a floating market, and some ports open their harbours to pirates for a share of the profit. An iguana parrot on the shoulder is a pirate captain's mark of status, crews often run in families, and tattoos are common among them. Pirate crews have always mixed people of every nation. To a pirate, a stranger with a full purse is cargo, and a stranger with something rare to sell is a customer until he is a fool. Anyone wanted ashore can find a berth on a pirate ship, if he can pay or fight.

lore.name: Pirate ship boutique
lore.info: Along rivers and coasts where the law is thin, some pirate crews tie up at a market pier and sell straight off the deck. The pirate ship boutique is the best known of these: a cargo hold turned into a shop, crowded with rare and exotic curios from every corner of the world, which the crew calls high-risk trading and everyone else calls theft. Selling from the ship keeps the deals private and keeps the sellers mobile, a step from casting off if the authorities come. A barker stands on the pier calling buyers in. Treasure hunters swear by it. Prices are what the pirates say they are, nothing is guaranteed, and nobody asks where anything came from.

lore.name: Pirates
lore.info: A pirate crew who scour the western seas for loot under a captain with an iguana parrot on his shoulder, selling their curiosities from their ship's deck when they dock at the river village and the seedy merchants pier: scrolls, charms, a monkey statue, and whatever the Fire Navy's cargo ships have lost. They would do almost anything for a reward. A stranger is a customer; a stranger with a purse is a mark; a stranger who steals is hunted. One sworn to the crew sails, steals, sells, and rises by what they bring aboard.

lore.name: Planetary calendar room
lore.info: Deep inside Wan Shi Tong's Library is the planetary calendar room, a round hall under a great dome that is, as a whole, a single machine. In its centre stands a control panel of ringed dials, the largest marked with the animals of the twelve-year cycle and others with the names of reigns and eras. Set the dials to a date and turn the crank, and gears beneath the floor move the heavens across the dome: crystal stars, the sun and the moon, each shown where it stood or will stand on that day. It was built by the library's keeper and his foxes from glowing crystal, jade and brass, and works on gears and cogs like a watch. Scholars who know of it call it a mechanical wonder. It reads the past and the future alike, which is exactly why its keeper is careful about who is shown the way in.

lore.name: Platypus bears on the river
lore.info: The platypus bear is a big brown river bear of the Earth Kingdom forests, with a white V on its chest, a wide duck's bill lined with jagged teeth, webbed hind feet and a broad flat tail it swims with and swings in a fight. It stands upright, hunts Se Tu fish above all and eats nearly anything else, people included. It is faster than it looks, and a mother with a cub is the worst danger on any river path. It lays eggs, and a frightened or furious platypus bear may drop one on the spot; the egg means it is upset, not that it is finished. Trained ones work in circuses and as guard beasts, as at the Full Moon Bay ferry, where one eats the condemned cabbages.

lore.name: Polar dogs of the South
lore.info: The polar dog is the pet of the Southern Water Tribe: a white animal the size of a big dog, built like a small bear, with blue eyes, a pink nose, rounded ears, three-toed paws and one black stripe running from the nose back over the forehead and down the spine. Its thick coat lets it sleep outside in a southern winter. Polar dogs are calm and patient with children; one will lie in the snow while a pack of shrieking youngsters climbs on it and barely open an eye. Nobody in the South has seen a wild one; every polar dog anyone knows of lives in a village, among people.

lore.name: Possum chicken
lore.info: The possum chicken lives in the Foggy Swamp: a white-feathered bird with wings and a chicken's body, but a possum's head and a long bare tail, and like a possum it hangs upside down by that tail from branches. The Foggy Swamp Tribe hunts it for the pot, and it is the meat they serve to guests. Swamp people compare any strange meat to it the way other people say a thing tastes like chicken, and they say so even about animals a traveller might be fond of. Outsiders who eat it at a swamp fire generally find it tastes like home.

lore.name: Purple pentapus
lore.info: The purple pentapus is a fist-sized creature with five arms, five eyes and a purple head, found in seas, lakes, rivers and even the sewer pipes of Omashu. It grips with strong suckers and hunts shellfish and algae. It is harmless, but once one fastens on a person it will not come off for pulling. The trick is to stroke the top of its head, which it loves; it lets go at once. The suckers leave a ring of red spots on the skin that fade after a while and look, to anyone who does not know, like an alarming rash. Anyone who has crawled through a drain should check his face before he walks past a guard.

lore.name: Quilled chameleon
lore.info: The quilled chameleon lives in the dense forests and jungles of the Earth Kingdom: a small dark-green reptile with lighter stripes, yellow eyes on either side of a peaked head, a long pink tongue and a tail kept rolled into a coil. Its front legs carry fans of sharp, feather-like quills. It changes colour to match the leaves and is very hard to spot. It hunts insects, crickets above all, with a flick of the tongue. It is shy, and a careful person can get close enough to feed it, but a grabbing hand gets a fistful of quills.

lore.name: Refugees of the war
lore.info: A century of war has put much of the Earth Kingdom on the road. Villages in the path of the Fire Army empty ahead of it, and whole tribes travel together with their elders and children toward Ba Sing Se, where the walls promise safety and the gates promise a long wait. The road east is hard: canyon guides charge for the crossing of the Great Divide, ferries charge for passage across the water, and the poor arrive with nothing. Some refugees never reach the capital at all. One group, driven from their valley by a flood, climbed into the Taihua Mountains and made their home in the empty Northern Air Temple. Travellers will meet refugee bands on every eastern road; most want only news, food and to be left alone.

lore.name: Riding and keeping ostrich horses
lore.info: The ostrich horse is the working mount of the Earth Kingdom: a bipedal, flightless bird-beast, coarse brown feathers on the body and tan hair on a horse-like head with a hooked beak, often a white or tan mane. Its long, powerful legs carry a rider fast over long distances, over high jumps and even a few strides up a wall. Couriers, merchants and farmers ride them or hitch them to carts and carriages, and in Ba Sing Se hired carriages behind ostrich horses cross the city. The army's cavalry mounts wear armour over the head, neck and flanks, and Fire Nation garrisons in the colonies keep them too. They are calm by nature but buck and kick when startled, so walk wide behind an unfamiliar one. Wild ones are solitary and often loiter near farms.

lore.name: Rough Rhinos
lore.info: An elite band of komodo rhino cavalry who ride for the Fire Lord on a freelance basis, paid by the job and loyal to the pay: a colonel, an archer, an explosives man, a chain fighter and a bender, each with his beast. They burn a town in an afternoon and are gone by night. They raid the southern coast and the plains and have ridden against Chin Village. A stranger is a target or a client; a foreigner is a target. One sworn to the Rough Rhinos rides, fights from the saddle, and rises by being the rider the colonel does not have to look back for.

lore.name: Royal Earthbender Guards
lore.info: The Earth King's personal protectors, earthbending warriors who belong to neither the army nor the Dai Li: they guard the Earth Kingdom Royal Palace, keep the gates of the Outer and Inner Walls, command the city's own troops and watch over everything the Earth King owns. They take their orders from the Council of Five. A stranger meets them at the gates with a passport in hand; a stranger without one meets them longer. One sworn to the guards keeps a gate or a palace door, and rises by never having let the wrong person through.

lore.name: Royal Gallery
lore.info: A long pillared hall inside the Fire Nation Royal Palace holds the portraits of the Fire Lords, each painted floor to ceiling and three times life size, each lord holding a ball of fire aloft to show his mastery, with scenes from his reign painted around him. Lanterns hang the length of the hall at even intervals, so every lord is lit alike. A single portrait can take the whole career of an artist to finish. Sozin, Azulon and Ozai hang there with the lords before them. The court calls it the nation's pride, and the story of each reign can be read from the wall behind its lord.

lore.name: Royal Procession
lore.info: The Fire Nation Royal Family's personal and ceremonial guard, an elite of firebenders in the skull masks and black armour that stand at every palace gate and ride with the Fire Lord's military moves. They guarded Azula's ship, they stand behind the throne, and they do not speak to anyone below a minister. A stranger sees them as a wall; a foreigner sees them as the last thing before the prison. One sworn to the Royal Procession guards the family with their body and their fire, and rises by being the one the family stands behind.

lore.name: Royal sloop
lore.info: A royal sloop is a royal-class Fire Nation ship kept for the use of the royal family, and each one is fitted out to its owner's taste. Some are massive and heavily ornamented to frighten whoever sees them come into port; others are built small and fast. They are among the most advanced ships of the Fire Navy, and the gilded rostrum on the prow is the same ornament the great battleships wear. A sloop's captain answers to the prince or princess aboard and to no admiral. When one docks, the harbour clears a berth and the town keeps its distance from the guards at the gangway.

lore.name: Sand-sailer
lore.info: The sandbenders of the Si Wong Desert cross the dunes on sand-sailers: light wooden craft on long runners, with a sail stretched between the hulls. A pilot bends whirling columns of sand behind the sail to make his own wind, so a sailer flies when the air is still. They carry few people and little cargo, but they are quick and nimble, and nothing else on the sand can catch them. Every sailer holds a compass that points not north but toward the great rock at the desert's heart, the one fixed mark in a sea of moving dunes. A traveller who finds a buried sailer has found a tribe's property, and the tribes do not forgive theft.

lore.name: Sandbending
lore.info: The tribes of the Si Wong Desert bend earth in its loosest form. Sandbenders ride wind-driven sand sailers across the dunes, shaping the sand beneath the runners into a road, and in a fight they can raise a blinding wall of grit or sink a man into a pit that fills as fast as he digs. The art grew from earthbending but looks little like the rooted stances of the cities; it is all sweeping arms and wide, shifting ground. Desert tribes guard their routes and their wells, and settle disputes among themselves. A traveller crossing the Si Wong without a sandbender guide is betting on a sky full of buzzard wasps.

lore.name: Schooling in the Fire Nation
lore.info: Fire Nation schools teach loyalty first. Children begin as soon as they can firebend, or as soon as they can walk if they cannot, and every day opens with the oath: a life given to the country, hands that fight for the Fire Lord and the forefathers before him, a mind that seeks to better the nation, feet that carry its march of civilization onward. Lessons cover etiquette, the nation's history, the history of warfare, music and firebending; the books teach that the war is the Fire Nation sharing its greatness, and that the Air Nomads raised an army against it. Dancing is frowned on as self-expression. Uniforms are strict: brown trousers or a skirt, a black and red vest, a red sash with the school's emblem, and no hats indoors. A child who will not behave is threatened with reform school, which means the coal mines.

lore.name: Se Tu fish
lore.info: The Se Tu fish is a big green river fish of the southern and western Earth Kingdom, with blue stripes along its sides, a long fin down its back, two short whiskers under its eyes and, people swear, thoughtful, almost human eyes. It can grow as long as a man. Se Tu like to leap clear of the water again and again, watching whoever is on the bank, and anglers take it as taunting. Once a year they swim hundreds of miles upriver to spawn. They are the platypus bear's favourite food, so a river full of jumping Se Tu is a river where bears hunt. Try to grab one barehanded and expect a slap from the tail.

lore.name: Seismic sense
lore.info: Badgermoles are blind, and they never need to see. They feel every tremor in the ground through their great paws, and know from it where the tunnel turns, where a rabbit hides, where a man is walking a mile off. As the first earthbenders, they are the first to have this sense, and earthbending masters still speak of it as the badgermoles' way of knowing the world. A few human benders have learned something of it: standing barefoot, quiet and still, and feeling footsteps through the earth. It is the deepest form of the listening that earthbending teaches. In the mountains where badgermoles dig, travellers learn to step softly; the creatures notice stamping, and do not like it.

lore.name: Shuhon Island
lore.info: Shuhon Island is the second largest of the Fire Islands, lying east of Capital Island, a rich island of fields and towns. Its best-known city is Fire Fountain City, a busy market and fairground town built where gas seeps out of the earth, famous for the giant statue of the Fire Lord that breathes real fire from its mouth over the main square. Announcements to the town are boomed out from the statue's mouth. Visitors from the other islands come for the fairs, the food stalls and the games of chance, and the town's guards keep a sharp eye on cheats. Like the rest of the home islands, the island has seen nothing of the war but its posters, its parades and its empty chairs.

lore.name: Si Wong tribes
lore.info: The people of the Si Wong Desert, loosely organised tribes of nomads, guides, traders, raiders and scavengers who bend loose sand instead of solid earth and cross the dunes on sand-sailers, effectively independent of the Earth Kingdom that stops at the desert's edge. A stranger with water is a guest; a stranger with a sky bison is a sale. One sworn to the tribes rides the sailers, learns the sand, and rises by the desert's own law, which is water given and water owed.

lore.name: Siege of Ba Sing Se
lore.info: No army has ever taken Ba Sing Se, and the Fire Nation's greatest attempt failed within living memory. General Iroh, Azulon's eldest son and heir, brought several armies to the Outer Wall and besieged the city for six hundred days. Fire Nation spies worked inside the walls while trebuchets battered them from outside, and at last his troops broke through the Outer Wall and fought their way into the farmland beyond. Then his son Lu Ten was killed. Iroh, grieving and with his army worn down by terrible losses, ordered a retreat; the defenders retook the ground and the wall was mended. Ba Sing Se counts it a victory, and many of its soldiers still curse his name. Fire Nation veterans who served under him call him a great leader, though at court the retreat is called weakness.

lore.name: Singing groundhog
lore.info: Colonies of singing groundhogs live in burrows on the wide prairies near the Si Wong Desert and in some mountain meadows. Each groundhog spends its life perfecting one single note. Play a tone on a flute and the groundhog whose note it is pops out of its hole and sings it back, nearly pitch-perfect, so a patient player can coax a whole song from a field. They are also harsh critics and duck back underground at a sour note. Travellers come from all over the world to hear them. Anyone planning the trip should know the groundhogs hibernate: in winter the prairie is silent and the holes are stopped up until spring.

lore.name: Sooty copper fritillary
lore.info: The sooty copper fritillary is a butterfly with orange wings shading to yellow at the edges and a brown body, found in the Earth Kingdom and the Fire Nation. It likes the dust around copper workings and flutters in clouds where copper lies near the surface. Prospectors know this and follow the butterflies to find new deposits; more than one fortune has begun with a man walking after a fritillary. That makes the butterfly itself sought after, and a miner who sees a cloud of them on someone else's claim will keep very quiet about it.

lore.name: South Pole continent
lore.info: The South Pole continent is the southernmost land in the world, frozen tundra and polar desert behind mountains no one climbs, almost all of it under snow. The Southern Water Tribe lives along its coast, because everything that feeds a southerner comes from the sea: fish, seals, sea prunes and the pelts that keep a family warm. Otter penguins nest on the shore in great colonies and tiger seals hunt them; a child of the South learns to sled on one and run from the other. The land has no timber, so the tribe has never had much of a fleet or much to trade. The raids of the war took the South's waterbenders one by one and left villages that are now little more than a wall of snow and a watchtower, and by 99 AG its fighting men have sailed away to the war. Visitors are rare. When a ship's smoke turns the snow grey, the villages hide what they can.

lore.name: South Sea
lore.info: The South Sea lies between the southern Earth Kingdom, the Air Nomads' old southern islands and the Southern Water Tribe. Its northern islands are tropical, its middle ones temperate, and its southernmost ones belong to the ice. Fishing is the trade of every shore: elephant koi off Kyoshi Island, and every fisherman's fear, the unagi. Close to the pole the water is cold enough to kill a swimmer within minutes, and icebergs drift through it the size of towns. Once the sea carried busy trade routes; the war made it a backwater. There is little here the Fire Navy wants, and only the Southern Raiders still sail it in strength, falling on the coasts of the South and of the southern Earth Kingdom. Pirates fill the gap the navies left, and a trader in these waters is never sure whether the ship hailing him is one.

lore.name: Southern Archipelago
lore.info: The Southern Archipelago is a chain of islands in the South Sea that were Air Nomad country, the land around the Southern Air Temple, which stands in the Patola Mountain Range on one of them. Other peoples have always lived on some of the islands, fishing and farming below the monks' mountains and trading with them. When the Air Nomads were wiped out at the start of the war, the islands lost the people who had given them their name. Some islands were resettled from other nations; others stand empty. Fire Nation soldiers have stayed in the archipelago ever since, occupying some islands, patrolling the slopes below the temple and raiding the villages that are not their own. Whaletail Island, shaped like the fluke of a whale, marks the chain's northern end. Islanders do not climb to the temple. They say it is empty, and that is all they say.

lore.name: Southern Raiders
lore.info: A Fire Navy special unit raised to raid the Southern Water Tribe, capture or kill its waterbenders and end any hope of resistance in the south, which it did, raid by raid, until the South had none left; it struck the Earth Kingdom's coast between raids. Its ships bring black snow before them. Its commanders retire to quiet villages. A stranger is of no interest to it; a Water Tribe stranger is. One sworn to the Southern Raiders sails south under sealed orders, does what the orders say, and rises by not asking what they were for.

lore.name: Southern Raiders frigate
lore.info: Southern Raiders frigates are the ships of the Fire Navy unit that hunted the South's waterbenders on Fire Lord Azulon's order. They are smaller, faster and handier than a cruiser, built to strike a shore and leave. A heavy bow breaks ice, a larger engine drives them, and paddle wheels take the place of the screws other ships use, because ice does not break a wheel as easily. Below decks there are quarters for long voyages and stores of weapons. Each one flies a red flag with a black sea raven. In the South, that flag on the horizon still empties a village.

lore.name: Southern Water Tribe
lore.info: The federation of the South Pole's small tribes, ruled by a council of elders who elect its chief, once thriving with a waterbending style of its own and now stripped of its benders by the Southern Raiders and of its men by the war: Hakoda's warriors have fought the Fire Navy from Chameleon Bay and the Black Cliffs since 97 AG, and Kanna keeps the village at Wolf Cove. A stranger is fed and asked for news of the men; a Fire Nation stranger is a prisoner if the children can manage it. One sworn to the tribe fights with Hakoda or keeps the village, and rises by the warriors' trust, which is given on the water.

lore.name: Southern Water Tribe raids
lore.info: More than sixty years ago the Fire Navy began to raid the South Pole, and it never fully stopped. The first raids came without warning: warships bombarded the walled ice cities, and waterbenders and warriors met them on the shore and sometimes won, trapping or wrecking ships in the ice. The Fire Nation wanted the South's waterbending gone, so each raid took more of the tribe's benders prisoner, and later raids were smaller because there was less left to fight. The captured waterbenders were carried away and never came home. The ice cities dwindled to villages, and the Southern Raiders were formed to finish the work. Southerners know the sign of an attack: black snow, soot falling with the flakes. The last raid, five years ago, came to Wolf Cove hunting the last waterbender and left a mother dead. Since then the Fire Nation has believed the South has no benders left.

lore.name: Sozin's Comet
lore.info: Once it was only the great comet: a fire that crosses the sky once in a hundred years and passes so close that its tail burns in the upper air. While it passes, every firebender beneath it holds a strength no training gives. A soldier's blast becomes a wall of flame; a master's becomes a storm. Fire Lord Sozin waited for its return. In the year it came, twelve years after Avatar Roku died, he loosed his empowered armies on the air temples, the western Earth Kingdom and both Water Tribes in a single season, and the Air Nomads did not survive it. The Fire Nation renamed the comet for him in honour of that victory, and its coming is the year from which the war is counted. The comet keeps its hundred-year road. It returns at the end of summer in 100 AG, and every general, sage and frightened villager who can count knows the date. What the Fire Lord means to do with that summer, no one outside his war room can say.

lore.name: Sozin's dragon
lore.info: Fire Lord Sozin rode a blue dragon, as fierce as its master and able to cover great distances at speed. Where Roku had a red dragon, Sozin had a blue one, and the Fire Nation remembers the pair of beasts as it remembers the two men. In later years the hunting of dragons became a path to honour in the Fire Nation, and the great beasts grew scarce. Nobody now living has seen a dragon carry a Fire Lord.

lore.name: Sozin's imperial campaign
lore.info: The war has an older root than the comet. Sozin and Avatar Roku were born on the same day and grew up as close as brothers, and Roku learned he was the Avatar at their shared sixteenth birthday. In 37 BG, with Roku away and Sozin newly Fire Lord, soldiers and settlers crossed to the western Earth Kingdom and planted the first Fire Nation colonies there, to share, the court said, the nation's prosperity with a poorer land. Fire Nation schools teach it as a generous beginning. What the Avatar thought of it is not taught at all; the court histories fall quiet on Roku's later years, and older courtiers speak of that time in lowered voices when they speak of it at all. The colonists stayed, and the oldest colonies on the western shore, with their Fire Nation streets and Earth Kingdom fields, date from that campaign.

lore.name: Sparrowkeet
lore.info: The sparrowkeet is the songbird of Ba Sing Se households: a dove-sized bird with lime-green feathers, a yellow head with white round the eyes and orange spots on the cheeks, an orange collar and a peach seed-cracking beak. Pet shops in the city keep them in cages and open bowls, and wild ones warble in the birdbaths of the university grounds. They are rowdy birds and jealous of their food. A sparrowkeet whose bowl is raided will squawk, flap and circle the thief's head with every other bird in the room joining in, and the shopkeeper will blame whoever brought the thief.

lore.name: Specialized bending techniques
lore.info: Each bending art has its rarer branches, learned only by those who have gone deep into the root art. Waterbenders heal. Desert tribes of the Si Wong bend sand into sails of wind and blinding storms. The swamp folk move water through the vines and roots of their trees. A few firebenders breathe fire from the mouth or call lightning, and a very few, marked with a third eye tattooed on the brow, can make fire explode at a distance with a thought; such a person is a hired weapon, and their mark is worth knowing on sight. Some branches are old and almost ordinary now; others are new, born with a single master and known to a handful of students.
